question: Two Sum: given an array and a target, return indices of two numbers that add up to the target.

followups.q: What if the array is already sorted?
followups.a: Then the hash map is unnecessary. Two pointers from both ends give O(1) extra space: if the sum is too large move the right pointer left, if too small move the left pointer right. Still O(n) time but no allocation, which also means far better cache behaviour. The catch is that it returns indices into the sorted array, so if the caller needs original indices you must pair values with their positions before sorting, which puts you back at O(n) space anyway.

followups.q: What if there can be more than one valid pair, and you must return all of them without duplicates?
followups.a: Sort first, then two-pointer, and when a pair is found advance both pointers past any runs of equal values so the same value pair is not emitted twice. The hash-map variant also works but needs a frequency count rather than a single index, plus a canonical ordering of each pair (smaller value first) to deduplicate. Sorting is O(n log n) but makes the deduplication trivial, so it is usually the cleaner answer here.

followups.q: What if the array does not fit in memory?
followups.a: It becomes an external problem. Either external sort into sorted runs and two-pointer stream from both ends, or partition by hash of the value so that a value and its complement always land in the same partition, then solve each partition in memory independently. The second option parallelises well and is the standard map-reduce shape for this class of problem.

followups.q: Why a Dictionary and not a HashSet here?
followups.a: Because the problem asks for indices, not values. A HashSet would confirm the complement exists but could not say where it was. If the required output were just a boolean or the value pair, a HashSet would be the better choice since it allocates less per entry.

question: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock: max profit from one buy and one later sell.

followups.q: What if unlimited transactions are allowed?
followups.a: It collapses to a much simpler problem: sum every positive daily difference, `max(0, prices[i] - prices[i-1])`, because any profitable multi-day run is exactly the sum of its consecutive upward steps. Still one pass, O(n) time, O(1) space, and no need to track buy and sell points at all. Candidates often reach for dynamic programming here, which works but is unnecessary.

followups.q: What if at most two transactions are allowed?
followups.a: Now the greedy break down and you need state. Track four values in one pass: the best balance after a first buy, after a first sell, after a second buy and after a second sell, updating each from the previous one. It stays O(n) time and O(1) space. That generalises to the k-transaction version as a two-dimensional DP over day and transaction count, which is O(nk), and when k exceeds n/2 it degenerates to the unlimited case above.

followups.q: What would you return for an empty array, and why not throw?
followups.a: Returning 0 is the right call because 'no transaction' is a legal outcome of the problem, not an error: the same reasoning that returns 0 for a strictly falling price series applies to an empty one. Throwing would force every caller into a try/catch for a case that has a perfectly sensible answer. A null input is more arguable, since that usually signals a caller bug rather than a real empty market, and some teams would want an ArgumentNullException there.

followups.q: Why update the profit before updating the minimum?
followups.a: Because buying and selling on the same day must yield 0, not a negative number. If the minimum is updated first and then used, the two values can refer to the same index, which is harmless here since the profit would be exactly 0, but the ordering makes the buy-strictly-before-sell constraint explicit rather than accidental. It matters more in the variants where the same slip produces a genuinely wrong answer.

question: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's algorithm): find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum.

followups.q: What if the interviewer asks you to return the subarray itself, not just the sum?
followups.a: Track the boundaries alongside the sums. Keep a `start` candidate that resets to `i` whenever `current` restarts from `nums[i]`, and when `best` is updated commit `bestStart = start` and `bestEnd = i`. The algorithm stays O(n) time and O(1) space; only three extra integers are needed. The subtlety is updating the recorded boundaries only when the global best actually improves, not on every iteration.

followups.q: What if the array is circular, so the subarray may wrap around the end?
followups.a: The answer is the maximum of two cases: the ordinary non-wrapping Kadane result, and `totalSum - minimumSubarraySum`, because the best wrapping subarray is the complement of the worst non-wrapping one. Run Kadane twice, once for max and once for min. The one trap is an all-negative array, where `totalSum - minSum` is 0 (the empty subarray) and must be rejected in favour of the plain Kadane answer.

followups.q: Could you solve it with divide and conquer, and would you?
followups.a: Yes: recursively solve left and right halves, then compute the best subarray crossing the midpoint by scanning outward from the centre, and take the maximum of the three. That is O(n log n). It is worth knowing because it is the shape used for segment-tree range queries, but as a standalone answer it is strictly worse than Kadane's O(n). Mention it as the generalisation, not the solution.

question: Product of Array Except Self (no division).

followups.q: Why is division disallowed, beyond it being an arbitrary rule?
followups.a: Because it breaks on zeros. With one zero, every other position is 0 and the zero position is the product of the rest, so you need a special case. With two or more zeros every position is 0, so you need a second special case. And dividing the total product by each element means the total can overflow even when no individual answer would. The prefix-suffix solution has none of those problems, which is why the constraint is really pointing you at the better algorithm rather than forbidding a shortcut.

followups.q: Is this really O(1) space when it allocates an output array?
followups.a: By the usual convention, yes: space required for the output does not count toward auxiliary space, since the problem demands it. The claim is that beyond the output you use only a constant number of variables, which is true here because the suffix product is one int rather than a second array. Say it that way in an interview, since claiming O(1) flatly while allocating an array invites a challenge you would then have to walk back.

followups.q: How would you handle overflow on large inputs?
followups.a: Products grow much faster than sums, so even a modest array of values around 1,000 overflows int within four elements. The options are to accumulate in `long` and document the assumption about input range, to use `System.Numerics.BigInteger` at a significant performance cost, or to work modulo some value if the problem asks for that. The critical part in an interview is naming the risk, because unlike the sum-based problems here it bites at realistic sizes, not just theoretical ones.

question: Find the missing number in an array containing 0..n with one missing.

followups.q: Why prefer XOR over the sum?
followups.a: Because it cannot overflow. The sum of 0 to n grows quadratically, so for n around 65,536 the total already exceeds int.MaxValue and an int accumulator wraps silently, giving a wrong answer with no exception. Using long, as above, fixes it for any realistic n, but XOR sidesteps the question entirely: every intermediate value stays within the range of the inputs. XOR also extends naturally to the harder variants where sums do not.

followups.q: What if two numbers are missing?
followups.a: The single equation is no longer enough, so you need two. Sum and sum-of-squares give a solvable pair of equations, though the squares overflow quickly. The cleaner route is XOR everything to get `a ^ b`, take any set bit of that result, which must be a bit where a and b differ, and partition all indices and values by that bit: XOR-ing each partition independently yields a and b separately. Same O(n) time and O(1) space, and it is the standard 'two single numbers' technique.

followups.q: What if you may modify the array and want to find it without arithmetic at all?
followups.a: Cyclic sort: walk the array placing each value v at index v by swapping, then scan for the first index whose value does not match. That is O(n) time and O(1) space, and it generalises to the whole family of problems where values are constrained to the range 0..n, including finding all missing numbers, finding duplicates, and finding the first missing positive. It is worth knowing as a pattern, since one implementation covers four common questions.

question: Move all zeros to the end while keeping non-zero order.

followups.q: Why not just remove the zeros and append them?
followups.a: Because building a new list allocates O(n) extra memory, and the problem asks for an in-place transform. It also changes the method's contract: the caller holds a reference to the original array and expects to see it modified, so returning a new array silently does nothing from their point of view. That mismatch between an in-place signature returning void and an implementation that builds a copy is a real bug, not a style preference.

followups.q: Which version would you ship, two-pass or swap?
followups.a: Usually the two-pass one. It touches memory sequentially in both passes, which is cache-friendly, and the second pass is a trivial fill the JIT can vectorise. The swap version looks cleverer but performs a redundant self-swap for every non-zero in an array with no zeros, meaning the common case of already-clean data costs the most. If the array is mostly zeros the swap version wins. Measure rather than assume, but the two-pass version is the safer default.

followups.q: How would you generalise this to move all elements failing an arbitrary predicate to the end?
followups.a: Replace `nums[read] != 0` with `predicate(nums[read])` and the fill value with whatever the caller supplies, or drop the second pass entirely and return the count of kept elements, which is exactly the partition primitive underlying `List<T>.RemoveAll` and C++'s `std::remove_if`. That framing, as a stable partition rather than a zero-moving trick, is what lets the same five lines solve a whole family of problems.

question: Container With Most Water: max area between two vertical lines.

followups.q: Prove that moving the taller pointer is safe to skip.
followups.a: Suppose the left line is shorter. Any container using that left line with a partner strictly inside the current right pointer has width less than the current width and height at most the current left height, since the left line caps it. So its area is strictly less than the area just computed. Every container involving the left line is therefore already accounted for, and the left line can be discarded. That exchange argument is what makes the two-pointer sweep complete rather than merely plausible, and it is what the interviewer wants to hear.

followups.q: How is this different from Trapping Rain Water, which looks similar?
followups.a: Container With Most Water picks exactly two lines and ignores everything between them, so the answer is a single rectangle. Trapping Rain Water sums the water sitting above every position, and the bars in between matter because they displace water. They share the two-pointer skeleton and the insight that the shorter side is the constraint, but the quantity accumulated is different: a maximum over pairs in one, a sum over positions in the other. Candidates who pattern-match on the picture rather than the quantity often answer the wrong one.

followups.q: What if the lines had non-zero thickness?
followups.a: Then the water displaced by the intervening bars matters and the greedy two-pointer no longer applies, since the volume is no longer just min-height times width. It becomes closer to the trapping-water formulation, where each position's contribution is computed against the bounding heights. It is worth saying out loud that the clean two-pointer answer depends on the problem's idealisation, because recognising which assumption the algorithm rests on is what makes it safe to reuse.

question: Trapping Rain Water: compute water trapped between bars.

followups.q: Why is it safe to settle a position using only one side's maximum?
followups.a: Because of the branch condition. When `leftMax <= rightMax`, there exists some bar on the right at least as tall as leftMax, so the true bound `min(maxLeft, maxRight)` must equal leftMax regardless of what else lies to the right. The unknown side cannot lower the bound below the known one. That is why the pointer comparison is on the running maxima rather than on the current heights, which is the detail most incorrect implementations get wrong.

followups.q: Solve it with a stack instead.
followups.a: Maintain a stack of decreasing bar indices. When a bar taller than the stack top arrives, it forms the right wall of a basin: pop the bottom of the basin, and with the new bar and the element now on top as walls, add the water for that horizontal layer. It accumulates water in layers rather than in columns, which is a genuinely different decomposition. Same O(n), but O(n) space. It is worth knowing because the same monotonic-stack shape solves largest rectangle in a histogram.

followups.q: What about the 2D version, trapping water on a heightmap?
followups.a: The one-dimensional reasoning fails, because water escapes through the lowest point on the whole boundary rather than along a single axis. The right approach is a min-heap seeded with all border cells, repeatedly popping the lowest boundary cell and flooding inward: any unvisited neighbour lower than the current water level traps the difference, and its own level becomes the maximum of the two. That is effectively Dijkstra over the boundary, at O(mn log(mn)), and it is a common follow-up for a strong candidate.

question: Rotate an array to the right by k steps in-place.

followups.q: Why the double modulo in ((k % n) + n) % n?
followups.a: Because C#'s `%` follows the sign of the dividend, so `-2 % 5` is -2, not 3. A single modulo therefore leaves a negative k, which would make the partial reversals index below zero. Adding n and taking the modulo again maps it into the range 0 to n-1 for any integer. It is the standard idiom whenever a modulus must be non-negative, and it comes up constantly in circular buffers and hash bucket indexing.

followups.q: What is the cyclic-replacement alternative?
followups.a: Move each element directly to its final position, following the cycle it belongs to, and repeat from the next unvisited start until n elements have moved. It touches each element exactly once rather than three times, so it is theoretically fewer writes. In practice it is harder to get right because the number of cycles is gcd(n, k) and the bookkeeping is fiddly, and its scattered memory access pattern often makes it slower than three cache-friendly sequential reversals despite doing less work.

followups.q: What if O(n) extra space were allowed?
followups.a: Then it is one line of intent: copy element i to position (i + k) % n in a new array, or use `Array.Copy` twice to move the two blocks. That is clearer and probably faster for moderate sizes, since it is two bulk memory moves rather than three passes of pairwise swaps. The in-place constraint is what makes the reversal trick necessary, and it is worth saying that you would take the simpler version unless memory genuinely mattered.

question: Merge two sorted arrays into one sorted array in-place (nums1 has extra space).

followups.q: Why does filling from the back work when filling from the front does not?
followups.a: Because the free space is at the back. Writing forward from index 0 would immediately overwrite nums1[0], which is still needed if nums2's first element is smaller. Writing backward, every destination index is at or beyond the position of the last unread element of nums1, so a write can only ever land on an empty slot or one already copied. That invariant, that the write pointer never overtakes the read pointer, is the whole argument and is worth stating explicitly.

followups.q: Why is the loop condition j >= 0 rather than i >= 0 || j >= 0?
followups.a: Because once nums2 is drained, every remaining element of nums1 is already sitting in its correct final position: it was never moved, and everything larger has been placed after it. Continuing to copy nums1 onto itself would be harmless but pointless work. The reverse is not true, which is why nums2 running out is the terminating condition and nums1 running out is handled by the `i >= 0` guard inside.

followups.q: Why does the caller pass m and n rather than using nums1.Length?
followups.a: Because nums1.Length is m + n, so the array cannot tell you where the real data ends and the padding begins. The trailing zeros are not sentinels: zero is a legitimate value. This is the same reason `List<T>` tracks Count separately from Capacity, and why APIs that take a buffer almost always take a length alongside it. Treating the padding as meaningful data is the mistake the signature is designed to prevent.

question: 3Sum: find all unique triplets that sum to zero.

followups.q: Why deduplicate by skipping rather than with a HashSet of triplets?
followups.a: A set works and is a legitimate fallback, but it costs memory proportional to the output and requires hashing each triplet, which means either a value tuple or a canonical string key. Skipping is free: the array is already sorted, so equal values are adjacent, and a comparison against the previous element is all that is needed. It also keeps the output naturally ordered. Reaching for a set is the sign of someone who has not noticed the sort already solved it.

followups.q: Generalise to 4Sum, or k-Sum.
followups.a: Recursively. k-Sum reduces to fixing one element and solving (k-1)-Sum on the remainder, bottoming out at 2-Sum with two pointers. That gives O(n^(k-1)), so 4Sum is O(n³). The same duplicate-skipping applies at every level. Write it as a recursive helper taking k and a starting index rather than nesting loops by hand, otherwise 4Sum becomes an unreadable four-deep nest and 5Sum is unwritable.

followups.q: Can 3Sum be solved faster than O(n²)?
followups.a: Not by any known general method. 3SUM is conjectured to require quadratic time, and that conjecture is used as a hardness assumption to prove lower bounds for a family of computational-geometry problems, which are called 3SUM-hard. There are slightly sub-quadratic results using clever bit tricks, but nothing that changes the practical picture. So O(n²) is the expected answer, and saying why no better one is expected is a strong close.

question: Find the majority element (appears more than n/2 times).

followups.q: Why is the verification pass necessary?
followups.a: Because the voting pass assumes a majority exists. Given [1,2,3,4] it returns whichever element happened to be last adopted, which is not a majority and not meaningful. Many published solutions omit the check because the problem statement promises a majority, but shipping that is a trap: the guarantee lives in the problem text, not in the code, and the first caller with unvalidated input gets a silently wrong answer instead of an error.

followups.q: Extend it to elements appearing more than n/3 times.
followups.a: There can be at most two such elements, so track two candidates and two counters with the same cancellation logic, then verify both at the end. The pattern generalises: for more than n/k there are at most k-1 candidates, needing k-1 counters, which is the Misra-Gries summary. The verification pass becomes mandatory rather than merely prudent, since with two candidates it is entirely possible that only one or neither actually qualifies.

followups.q: What if the data is a stream too large to store?
followups.a: Boyer-Moore already handles it: it is one pass with O(1) memory and never revisits an element. The catch is the verification pass, which needs a second read of the stream. If the stream can only be read once, you cannot verify exactly, and the honest answers are either to accept the candidate under an assumed guarantee or to use a Count-Min Sketch for approximate frequencies with a bounded error. That constraint, one pass versus two, is what the question is usually driving at.

question: Find the median of two sorted arrays in O(log(min(m,n))).

followups.q: Why binary search the shorter array specifically?
followups.a: Because the complexity is logarithmic in whatever you search, so searching the shorter one gives O(log(min(m,n))) rather than O(log(max(m,n))). It also guarantees the derived index j stays within the longer array's bounds, which would need extra guarding otherwise. Swapping at the top costs nothing and removes a whole class of edge cases. If one array is tiny and the other is enormous, this is the difference between a handful of iterations and dozens.

followups.q: What are the int.MinValue and int.MaxValue sentinels for?
followups.a: They represent 'nothing on that side', so a cut at the very start or end of an array needs no special branch: a missing left neighbour compares as smaller than everything, a missing right neighbour as larger. That collapses four edge cases into the ordinary comparison. It is the acceptable use of in-band sentinels because the comparison is directional rather than an equality test, though if the data could legitimately contain int.MinValue you would widen to long, exactly as in the BST validation problem.

followups.q: Why half = (m + n + 1) / 2 rather than (m + n) / 2?
followups.a: The +1 biases the extra element to the left partition when the total is odd, which means the median is simply the largest element on the left and needs no separate case. Without it, an odd total would leave the median on the right and the two branches would differ more than necessary. It is a small choice that makes the odd and even cases share almost all their code, and getting it wrong produces answers that are off by one position on odd inputs only.

followups.q: Suppose you only needed an approximate median over a stream.
followups.a: Then this is the wrong tool entirely, since it needs both arrays materialised and sorted. For streaming you would use two heaps to maintain an exact running median, or for very large volumes a t-digest or reservoir sample for an approximation with bounded error and constant memory. Naming the constraint that changes the answer, batch and sorted versus streaming and unbounded, is more valuable than the binary search itself.

question: Search in a rotated sorted array.

followups.q: What breaks when duplicates are allowed?
followups.a: The sortedness test does. With [1,0,1,1,1] the low, mid and high values are all 1, so you cannot tell which half is sorted. The standard fix is that when `nums[low] == nums[mid] == nums[high]` you cannot decide, so you shrink the range by one from each end and continue. That makes the worst case O(n), for example an array of all equal values, and no better bound is possible: an adversary can hide the target behind an indistinguishable run.

followups.q: Would you instead find the pivot first and then binary search?
followups.a: It is a perfectly good answer and often easier to get right: one binary search to locate the minimum, which is the rotation point, then a normal binary search in the correct segment, or a single search over the whole array with index arithmetic modulo the length. It is two passes of O(log n), so the same complexity. The one-pass version above is tighter, but under interview pressure the two-step version has fewer conditions to get backwards, and being able to explain both is the strongest position.

followups.q: Why compare nums[low] <= nums[mid] rather than nums[mid] <= nums[high]?
followups.a: Either works as long as you are consistent and handle the equality correctly, but the low comparison needs `<=` rather than `<` for the two-element case where low and mid are the same index. Choosing one and deriving the four range conditions from it is what matters. Mixing the two conventions mid-solution is how this problem usually goes wrong, and it produces bugs that only appear on specific rotations, which are miserable to find under time pressure.

question: Find first and last position of a target in a sorted array.

followups.q: Why does the lower bound use an exclusive high and low < high?
followups.a: Because the answer may legitimately be 'past the last element', which an inclusive high cannot represent. With `high = nums.Length` and the loop condition `low < high`, the search converges on an insertion point in the range 0 to n inclusive, which is exactly what a lower bound means. Mixing the inclusive and exclusive conventions within one function is the usual way binary searches go wrong, so picking one and deriving every bound from it is the discipline that matters.

followups.q: Why search for target + 1 rather than writing a separate upper-bound search?
followups.a: Because it reuses the one primitive you have already got right, and the first index greater than the target is by definition the lower bound of target + 1. Writing a second search with subtly different comparisons doubles the chance of an off-by-one. The one caveat is overflow: if the target were int.MaxValue then target + 1 wraps, so production code would either use long or write the upper bound explicitly. Worth mentioning, since it is a real edge case the reuse introduces.

followups.q: Suppose you needed the count of occurrences rather than the positions.
followups.a: It falls straight out: last minus first plus one, or equivalently the lower bound of target + 1 minus the lower bound of target, which needs no presence check at all and returns zero naturally when absent. That subtraction form is the cleaner implementation and generalises to counting elements in any value range, which is a common requirement when bucketing sorted data.

question: Set matrix zeroes: if an element is 0, set its entire row and column to 0, in-place.

followups.q: Why does the application pass run backwards?
followups.a: Because the first row and first column hold the markers, and writing them early would destroy information still needed for later cells. Working from the bottom-right inward means every cell is written only after its row and column markers have been consumed. Going forwards, zeroing cell [0][1] as part of applying row 0 would erase the marker saying 'column 1 has a zero' before the rest of that column is processed. The direction is load-bearing, not stylistic.

followups.q: Why does the first column need a separate flag?
followups.a: Because matrix[0][0] is shared: it is the row marker for row 0 and the column marker for column 0 at the same time, so a single cell cannot distinguish which of the two conditions set it. Splitting one of them out into an ordinary boolean resolves the ambiguity. You could equally give the first row its own flag instead; what you cannot do is use the origin for both. Missing this produces a matrix that is correct except for one row or column, which is easy to overlook.

followups.q: Would you actually use the O(1)-space version?
followups.a: Usually not. The two-set version is a few lines, obviously correct, and costs O(rows + cols), which next to the O(rows x cols) matrix you already hold is a rounding error. The in-place version trades clear code for a saving that is proportional to the square root of the data size. I would reach for it only if the matrix were so large that even the linear overhead mattered, and I would comment the backwards pass heavily, since the next reader will assume it is arbitrary.

question: Spiral order traversal of a matrix.

followups.q: Why do the bottom and left walks need an extra boundary check when the first two do not?
followups.a: Because the loop condition was verified before the top walk, but the top and right walks each shrink a boundary, so by the time the bottom walk starts the layer may have been fully consumed. A single-row matrix is the clearest case: the top walk takes the whole row and increments top past bottom, and without the re-check the bottom walk would traverse that same row backwards and emit every element twice. The single-row and single-column tests exist for exactly this.

followups.q: Is there a way to avoid the four boundaries?
followups.a: Yes, a direction-vector approach: move in the current direction until the next cell is out of bounds or already visited, then turn right. It needs a visited grid or a sentinel value, which costs O(rows x cols) space unless you may mutate the input. The boundary version is O(1) space and avoids the visited check entirely, so it is generally preferred, though the direction version generalises more easily to spirals in other shapes or to generating a spiral rather than reading one.

followups.q: Suppose you had to generate a spiral matrix rather than read one.
followups.a: It is the same boundary walk with the assignment reversed: instead of appending matrix[r][c] to a list, you write an incrementing counter into it. The loop structure and the two re-checks are identical. That symmetry is worth pointing out, because interviewers sometimes ask the generation version expecting a fresh approach, and recognising it as the same traversal makes it a two-minute answer instead of a restart.

question: Rotate an n×n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in-place.

followups.q: Why transpose only the upper triangle?
followups.a: Because each swap exchanges a pair, so visiting both [r][c] and [c][r] performs the same swap twice and restores the original. Starting the inner loop at `r + 1` visits each pair exactly once and also skips the diagonal, which needs no swap. Running the inner loop from 0 is the standard bug and produces a matrix identical to the input, which looks like the function did nothing rather than like a logic error.

followups.q: Why does transpose-then-reverse equal a rotation?
followups.a: A transpose is a reflection across the main diagonal, and reversing each row is a reflection across the vertical axis. Composing two reflections whose axes meet at 45 degrees gives a rotation of twice that angle, which is 90 degrees. That also explains the anticlockwise variant: reflecting across the diagonal and then across the horizontal axis rotates the other way. Knowing the composition rule means you can derive the right pair of steps rather than memorising four cases.

followups.q: What changes for a non-square matrix?
followups.a: Rotation is no longer possible in place, because an m by n matrix becomes n by m, so the storage shape itself changes. You must allocate a new matrix with the dimensions swapped and copy, which is O(mn) time and space. That is worth stating explicitly, since the in-place requirement in the problem quietly depends on squareness and candidates sometimes claim their solution generalises when it cannot.

followups.q: How would you rotate by 180 or 270 degrees?
followups.a: 180 is two 90-degree rotations, but more cheaply it is a reverse of the row order combined with a reverse of each row, with no transpose at all. 270 clockwise is the same as 90 anticlockwise. Applying the 90 rotation repeatedly is simplest and the four-rotations test above confirms it returns to the original, but for a large matrix the direct formulations avoid redundant passes over the data.

question: Maximum product subarray.

followups.q: Why must the minimum be tracked as well as the maximum?
followups.a: Because multiplication by a negative turns the smallest value into the largest. In [-2, 3, -4] the running minimum before the last element is -6, and multiplying by -4 gives 24, which is the answer; a maximum-only algorithm never sees it. Kadane's sum version needs no minimum because addition preserves order: adding a number cannot turn the worst running total into the best. The sign-flip is precisely what makes products harder than sums.

followups.q: What exactly goes wrong if you assign currentMax before computing currentMin?
followups.a: The minimum calculation would use the new maximum rather than the previous one, so it is comparing against a value from the wrong step. The result is subtly wrong only on inputs where the swap matters, meaning arrays containing negatives, so it passes all-positive tests cleanly. Using temporaries and assigning both afterwards is the fix, and it is the same class of error as updating a rolling DP variable before the value it depends on has been read.

followups.q: Suppose the array could contain zeros and you wanted the maximum product of a non-empty subarray excluding zeros.
followups.a: Zeros already act as natural separators, since both running values reset through them, so the algorithm effectively restarts on each segment and takes the best across all of them. If zeros had to be excluded from the answer entirely, you would split the array on zeros and run the algorithm per segment, which is the same work. The more interesting variant is when the answer may be empty, in which case you would clamp at zero, and it is worth asking which convention applies.

followups.q: What about overflow?
followups.a: Products grow far faster than sums, so an array of a dozen values near a thousand overflows int, and the code above would silently wrap. LeetCode constrains the inputs so it does not arise, which is a bad habit to absorb. In real code you would accumulate in long and still document a bound, or use checked arithmetic so it throws rather than producing a plausible wrong answer. Naming the risk is worth more than the algorithm here, because unlike the sum version it bites at realistic sizes.

question: Check if a string is a palindrome (ignoring non-alphanumerics and case).

followups.q: Why ToLowerInvariant rather than ToLower?
followups.a: Because `ToLower` uses the current culture, and in Turkish the uppercase of `i` is a dotted capital, not `I`. That means the same string can be judged a palindrome on one machine and not on another purely from the thread's culture setting. Any comparison that is about character identity rather than about presenting text to a user should be culture-invariant or ordinal. It is a classic production bug, not a theoretical one.

followups.q: What if the string can contain characters outside the basic multilingual plane, like emoji?
followups.a: Then indexing by `char` is wrong, because a `char` in .NET is a UTF-16 code unit and such characters occupy a surrogate pair. Reversing or comparing by code unit would split the pair and produce nonsense. The fix is to iterate by rune, using `StringInfo.GetTextElementEnumerator` or `System.Text.Rune`, which also handles combining marks where one visible character is several code points. For the alphanumeric-only version here the point is somewhat academic, since surrogates are not letters or digits in the ASCII sense, but it is the right thing to raise.

followups.q: How would you check whether a linked list is a palindrome, where you cannot index?
followups.a: Find the middle with a slow and fast pointer, reverse the second half in place, then walk the two halves together comparing values. That is O(n) time and O(1) space. The courteous touch is to restore the list by reversing the second half back before returning, since a predicate that silently mutates its input is a nasty surprise. The alternative of copying values into a list and using two pointers is O(n) space and usually considered the weaker answer.

question: Check if two strings are anagrams.

followups.q: If the input is guaranteed lowercase ASCII, can you do better?
followups.a: Yes: replace the dictionary with `int[26]` indexed by `c - 'a'`. That removes hashing entirely, fits in a cache line, and typically runs several times faster for short strings. It is the answer worth giving when the interviewer states the constraint, but say out loud that it is only valid because of that constraint, since silently assuming a 26-letter alphabet is exactly the kind of thing that breaks on real input.

followups.q: How does this change for Unicode?
followups.a: Two ways. First, counting by `char` breaks for characters outside the basic multilingual plane, so you would count runes instead. Second, and more subtly, the same visible text can have several encodings: 'é' as one code point, or as 'e' plus a combining accent. Two strings that look identical would then count differently. The fix is to normalise both with `string.Normalize(NormalizationForm.FormC)` before counting, which is a detail almost nobody raises unprompted and lands well when you do.

followups.q: You need to group many strings into anagram sets. What changes?
followups.a: Pairwise comparison is O(n^2) comparisons, so instead compute a canonical key per string and group on it. The sorted characters make a serviceable key, at O(k log k) per string, or a 26-entry count vector rendered to a string gives an O(k) key. Then a single dictionary from key to list does the grouping in one pass. That is the Group Anagrams problem, and recognising that it is the same counting insight applied as a key is the point.

followups.q: Why check the lengths first when the counting loop would catch it anyway?
followups.a: Because it would not, in general. The decrementing loop only detects that `t` has a character `s` lacks; if `s` were longer, every character of `t` could still be present and the method would wrongly return true, since nothing verifies the counts ended at zero. The length check is what makes the final `return true` sound, which is worth stating rather than treating it as a mere optimisation.

question: Longest substring without repeating characters.

followups.q: How would you return the substring itself rather than its length?
followups.a: Record the start index whenever the best length improves, then slice once at the end with `s.Substring(bestStart, best)`. Two extra integers, no change in complexity. The thing to avoid is building the candidate substring on every iteration, which quietly turns an O(n) algorithm into O(n^2) through allocation and copying, and is a common way to fail a follow-up that looks trivial.

followups.q: What if at most k distinct characters were allowed rather than zero repeats?
followups.a: The window becomes count-based instead of index-based: hold a dictionary of character to count within the window, and while the dictionary has more than k entries, shrink from the left, decrementing counts and removing entries that reach zero. Still O(n), since each character enters and leaves at most once. It is the same sliding-window skeleton, and recognising that the two problems share it is more valuable than either solution alone.

followups.q: Could you avoid the dictionary entirely?
followups.a: If the alphabet is bounded, yes: an `int[128]` or `int[256]` of last-seen indices, initialised to -1, removes all hashing and is noticeably faster. State the assumption when you do it, because it silently breaks on non-ASCII input. For arbitrary Unicode the dictionary is the honest choice, and if surrogate pairs are in play you would be iterating runes rather than chars anyway.

question: Group anagrams together from a list of strings.

followups.q: Why the '#' separator in the count key?
followups.a: Without it the counts run together and different inputs can produce the same key. A string with 1 'a' and 11 'b's gives "111..." and so does one with 11 'a's and 1 'b'. Concatenating variable-length numbers without a delimiter is a general hazard, and the same class of bug appears when people build cache keys or hashes by string concatenation. The separator makes the encoding unambiguous.

followups.q: Sorted key or count key: which would you use?
followups.a: The sorted key, usually. It is three lines, obviously correct, works for any alphabet including Unicode, and for typical word lengths the log factor is irrelevant. The count key wins only when strings are long and the alphabet is small and fixed, and it silently breaks on any character outside a-z, which is a nasty failure since it indexes out of the array or corrupts a neighbouring count. Simplicity first, and switch if profiling says so.

followups.q: Is the output order guaranteed?
followups.a: No. Dictionary enumeration order in .NET is unspecified and must not be relied on, even though it often looks insertion-ordered in practice. If the caller needs deterministic output, sort the groups explicitly by some stable criterion before returning. Tests that assert an exact group order without sorting are a well-known source of failures that appear only after an unrelated change, which is worth flagging when you write them.

question: Longest palindromic substring.

followups.q: Why does the length come out as right - left - 1?
followups.a: Because the while loop only stops after a failed comparison, so when it exits `left` is one before the palindrome's first character and `right` is one past its last. The inclusive span is therefore `(left+1)` to `(right-1)`, whose length is `(right-1) - (left+1) + 1`, which simplifies to `right - left - 1`. Off-by-one errors here are the single most common way this solution breaks, so deriving it out loud rather than recalling it is worth doing.

followups.q: Is there a linear-time solution?
followups.a: Manacher's algorithm, which is O(n). It reuses the palindrome radii already computed on the left of a known centre to skip work on the right, in the same spirit as the KMP failure function. It is rarely expected in an interview and is hard to reproduce correctly under pressure, so the right move is to name it, say that expansion is O(n²) and that Manacher's brings it to O(n), and offer to write it only if they want it.

followups.q: How does this differ from the longest palindromic subsequence?
followups.a: Completely. A substring is contiguous, a subsequence is not, so the subsequence version cannot use centre expansion at all. It is a two-dimensional DP over the string and its reverse, equivalent to the longest common subsequence of s and reverse(s), at O(n²) time and space. The names are close enough that candidates answer the wrong question, so the first thing to do is confirm which one is being asked.

question: Valid parentheses: check if brackets are balanced.

followups.q: The ContainsValue call is O(n) on the dictionary. Does that matter?
followups.a: Here the dictionary has three entries, so it is a constant with a small factor and the method is still O(n) overall. But it is sloppy, and an interviewer may well probe it. The clean fix is a `switch` on the three opening characters, or a second small set of openers, which makes the classification O(1) and reads better. It is worth noticing out loud even when the cost is negligible, because the habit is what is being assessed.

followups.q: What if the string also contains ordinary text, not only brackets?
followups.a: The code above already handles it: a character that is neither an opener nor a closer falls through both branches and is ignored. That is deliberate and worth pointing out, since a version written with `else return false` would reject any real expression. If the requirement is stricter and only bracket characters are legal input, then the explicit rejection belongs there instead, and the difference should be a stated assumption rather than an accident.

followups.q: How would you extend this to report where the error is, as an editor would?
followups.a: Push the index alongside the character, so the stack holds positions as well as bracket types. On a mismatch you can then report both the offending closer's index and the index of the opener it failed to match, and on leftovers you report the position of each unclosed opener rather than only that the count was wrong. Same complexity, and it is the shape real parsers use, since a message saying 'unbalanced' with no position is nearly useless in a large file.

followups.q: Could this be done without a stack?
followups.a: With a single bracket type, yes: a counter that increments on open and decrements on close, failing if it ever goes negative and requiring zero at the end. With multiple types it cannot, because the counter loses the ordering information that distinguishes `([)]` from `([])`. That contrast is a neat way to show why the problem genuinely needs a stack, which is usually what the interviewer is checking.

question: String to integer (atoi) with edge cases.

followups.q: Why clamp inside the loop rather than after it?
followups.a: Because a long overflows too. An input of forty digits would overflow the long accumulator long before the loop ends, wrapping to some arbitrary value that might even look valid, so a single check at the end cannot save you. Clamping on every iteration bounds the accumulator permanently. The general lesson is that widening the type only buys headroom, it does not remove the overflow case, so the check has to be inside the loop that grows the value.

followups.q: Why write this at all when int.TryParse exists?
followups.a: In production you would use `int.TryParse`, and saying so is the right instinct. The behaviours differ though: TryParse rejects trailing garbage rather than stopping at it, returns false instead of clamping on overflow, and is culture-sensitive by default, so it accepts thousands separators and locale-specific signs. This problem specifies C's atoi semantics, which are deliberately permissive. The interview value is that the edge cases here are exactly the ones any real parser must decide on.

followups.q: Why char.IsAsciiDigit rather than char.IsDigit?
followups.a: Because `char.IsDigit` returns true for decimal digits in every script, including Arabic-Indic and Devanagari numerals. Subtracting '0' from those produces nonsense, so the parse would silently compute a garbage value rather than stopping. `IsAsciiDigit`, added in .NET 7, says exactly what is meant. It is a small example of a wider rule: when a routine assumes ASCII, assert ASCII rather than relying on a broader predicate that happens to work for the inputs you tested.

question: Find all anagrams of a pattern in a string.

followups.q: Why is the matches counter updated with those two specific conditions?
followups.a: Because a letter's contribution changes only at the boundary. When a count rises to exactly the needed value, that letter has just become correct, so matches increases. When it rises to one above, it has just stopped being correct, so matches decreases. Every other increment moves between two wrong values and changes nothing. The removal side mirrors it. Reasoning at the transition rather than recomputing is what makes the update O(1), and it is the same idea as maintaining a running aggregate in any sliding window.

followups.q: Why is this window fixed while the minimum-window-substring one is elastic?
followups.a: Because an anagram must use exactly the pattern's characters with exactly its multiplicities, which pins the length. Minimum window asks for a superset, so extra characters are permitted and the window must be free to grow and shrink to find the tightest valid span. The 'exactly' versus 'at least' distinction is what decides between a fixed and an elastic window, and spotting it from the problem statement saves a lot of wrong turns.

followups.q: The int[26] assumes lowercase ASCII. What would you do otherwise?
followups.a: Switch to a dictionary keyed by character and replace `matches == 26` with a comparison against the number of distinct required characters, tracking how many of those are satisfied. That keeps the O(1) update while removing the alphabet assumption, at the cost of hashing. The array version is genuinely faster when the constraint holds, so I would keep it and assert the assumption rather than leave it implicit, since `c - 'a'` on an unexpected character indexes out of bounds or silently corrupts a neighbouring count.

question: Minimum window substring containing all characters of a pattern.

followups.q: Why is the need count allowed to go negative?
followups.a: Because a negative value records a surplus: the window holds more copies of that character than required. That surplus is exactly what lets the left edge advance without breaking validity, and the `have + 1 > 0` test on removal distinguishes giving up a surplus copy, which is free, from giving up a required one, which invalidates the window. Clamping the count at zero loses that information and the shrink loop stops too early, producing windows that are valid but not minimal.

followups.q: Why track a single missing counter rather than comparing the two maps?
followups.a: Because a map comparison is O(alphabet) and would run on every one of the n steps, making the algorithm O(n x alphabet) rather than O(n). The counter compresses the entire validity question into one integer by exploiting the fact that validity changes by at most one character per step. That pattern, maintaining an aggregate rather than recomputing a predicate, is the general technique behind most efficient sliding-window solutions.

followups.q: Suppose duplicates in the pattern had to be matched exactly, not at least.
followups.a: Then a surplus would make the window invalid rather than merely wasteful, so the shrink condition changes from 'still valid' to 'exactly matching', and the window can no longer grow freely past a surplus. In practice that becomes the fixed-length window of the anagram-search problem, since an exact multiset match forces the window length to equal the pattern length. It is a good illustration that 'at least' and 'exactly' produce genuinely different algorithms from nearly identical statements.

question: Implement strStr / substring search (find needle in haystack).

followups.q: Explain what the LPS table means, using aabaaac.
followups.a: Each entry is the length of the longest proper prefix of that position's prefix which is also its suffix. At index 4, the prefix is "aabaa", whose longest border is "aa", so the entry is 2. That means if a mismatch happens after matching five characters, two of them are already re-matched by shifting, so comparison resumes at needle index 2 without moving back in the haystack. The table encodes what the needle knows about its own self-similarity, which is why no re-examination is ever needed.

followups.q: Is KMP what a real library uses?
followups.a: Usually not. .NET's `IndexOf` uses vectorised SIMD scanning, and many libraries use Boyer-Moore or a hybrid, because Boyer-Moore can skip ahead by the needle length on a mismatch and is sub-linear on typical text, which beats KMP's guaranteed linearity in the average case. KMP's value is its worst-case bound and the fact that it never backs up in the input, which makes it the right choice for streaming data you cannot rewind.

followups.q: Why does an empty needle return 0 rather than -1?
followups.a: By convention, the empty string is found at every position, so the first occurrence is index 0. It matches `string.IndexOf("")` in .NET and the equivalent in most languages. It is worth calling out explicitly because it is an arbitrary convention rather than a derivable fact, and an interviewer asking about it is checking whether you clarify undefined behaviour rather than silently picking one.

question: Encode and decode strings (serialize a list of strings).
answer: Length-prefix encoding: for each string, write its length, a delimiter, then the string (e.g., '5#hello'). To decode, read the length up to the delimiter, then read exactly that many characters. This handles any characters including the delimiter. O(n) time.

question: Reverse words in a string.

followups.q: Why not just Split, Reverse and Join?
followups.a: You can, and `string.Join(" ", s.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries).Reverse())` is one readable line that I would happily ship. The reason the manual version exists is memory: Split allocates an array plus a string per word, so a large input creates substantial garbage, whereas the StringBuilder version allocates once. In an interview the one-liner is the right first answer, followed by the manual version when they ask you to avoid the intermediate allocations.

followups.q: How does the three-reversal trick relate to rotating an array?
followups.a: It is the same identity: reversing the whole thing and then reversing the pieces restores internal order while moving the blocks. Array rotation reverses two fixed-size blocks; word reversal reverses variable-length blocks delimited by spaces. Recognising that one technique covers both, and also the in-place rotation of a matrix by transpose-then-reverse, is more valuable than memorising three separate tricks.

followups.q: What about Unicode text, where words are not just space-delimited?
followups.a: Then splitting on the space character is wrong. Some scripts do not use spaces between words at all, and others use non-breaking or ideographic spaces that this code would treat as part of a word. Correct word segmentation needs the Unicode text-segmentation rules, available through `System.Globalization.StringInfo` for graphemes or a proper ICU-backed library for word boundaries. It is worth flagging, because 'reverse the words' quietly assumes an English-shaped world.

question: Count and Say / run-length encoding of a string.
answer: Iterate counting consecutive equal characters; append count + character to the result and reset when the character changes. O(n) time. Run-length encoding compresses runs; useful for strings with many repeats (poor for high-entropy data).

question: Check if one string is a rotation of another.
answer: s2 is a rotation of s1 iff they have the same length and s2 is a substring of s1+s1 (concatenate s1 with itself, then check contains(s2)). O(n) with an efficient substring search. Elegant single-check solution.

question: Longest common prefix among an array of strings.

followups.q: Why StringComparison.Ordinal on StartsWith?
followups.a: Because the default overload is culture-sensitive, which is both slower and semantically wrong here. Culture-aware comparison applies linguistic rules: certain sequences compare as equal to others, and zero-width characters can be ignored entirely, so two strings that differ by code point can be reported as a prefix match. For structural comparison of identifiers, paths or keys, always use Ordinal. This is one of the most common performance and correctness defects in real .NET code.

followups.q: Which scan direction is better?
followups.a: The vertical scan usually. It stops at the very first differing character, so a set of strings that diverge immediately costs O(n) rather than requiring any string manipulation, and it allocates only the final substring. The horizontal version allocates a new string on every shrink step, which for a long first string and an early mismatch means many wasted allocations. Both are O(S) in the worst case, but the constants differ noticeably.

followups.q: What if you must answer this repeatedly for many query sets?
followups.a: Build a trie of all the strings once; the longest common prefix is then the path from the root down to the first node that either branches or marks the end of a word. The build is O(S), and each query becomes proportional to the prefix length rather than to the total input. That is the right structure whenever prefix questions are asked repeatedly, which is exactly why autocomplete and routing tables are built on tries.

question: Regular expression matching with '.' and '*'.
answer: Dynamic programming: dp[i][j] = does s[0..i) match p[0..j). '.' matches any char; '*' matches zero or more of the preceding element (dp[i][j] = dp[i][j-2] for zero, or match preceding and dp[i-1][j]). Fill the table bottom-up. O(n*m) time and space.

question: Subarray sum equals k (count subarrays).

followups.q: Why must the map be seeded with {0: 1}?
followups.a: Because a subarray that starts at index 0 has no earlier prefix to subtract. If the running sum reaches exactly k at index j, the matching earlier prefix is 0, which corresponds to the empty prefix before the array began. Without the seed that lookup fails and every such subarray is missed. It is the single most common bug in this problem, and it only shows up when the answer includes a prefix of the array, so weak test data hides it.

followups.q: Why can't you use a sliding window, as you would for 'minimum length subarray with sum at least k'?
followups.a: Sliding windows rely on monotonicity: extending the window must move the sum in one direction so that shrinking can correct an overshoot. That holds when all values are positive, and fails the moment negatives are allowed, because extending can decrease the sum. So the window has no valid shrink rule. Whenever a subarray-sum problem permits negative values, prefix sums with a map is the pattern, and recognising which of the two applies is what the interviewer is testing.

followups.q: How does 'subarray sums divisible by k' change this?
followups.a: Key the map on `sum % k` rather than the sum itself, because two prefixes with the same remainder bound a subarray whose sum is a multiple of k. The catch is negative remainders: in C# `-3 % 5` is -2, not 3, so you must normalise with `((sum % k) + k) % k` or the two representations of the same residue class never match. That is the same signed-modulo trap as in array rotation.

followups.q: Why accumulate into a long?
followups.a: Because the running prefix sum can exceed int range even when no individual element does: a million elements near int.MaxValue/2 overflow long before the end. An overflowed prefix wraps and can coincidentally match a lookup, producing a wrong count with no error. Widening the accumulator costs nothing here and removes a failure mode that only appears on large inputs, which is exactly the kind that reaches production untested.

question: Longest consecutive sequence in an unsorted array.

followups.q: Prove this is O(n) despite the nested while loop.
followups.a: The inner walk only ever runs from a value whose predecessor is absent, so each run is walked exactly once in total, no matter how many members it has. Every element is therefore touched at most twice: once by the outer loop and once as part of its own run's single walk. That bounds the total work at 2n set lookups, which is linear. Without the `set.Contains(n - 1)` guard the same run would be re-walked from each member and the worst case would be quadratic, which is the whole reason that one line exists.

followups.q: Does iterating the set rather than the array matter?
followups.a: Yes, for duplicates. Iterating the original array would repeat the work for every copy of a value, so an array of a million identical numbers would do a million outer iterations instead of one. It does not break correctness because the guard still prevents the inner walk, but it wastes time proportional to the duplication. Iterating the set makes the bound hold on the distinct count rather than the raw length.

followups.q: How would you return the sequence itself, or handle a stream?
followups.a: For the sequence, record the starting value whenever the best length improves; the run is then start to start+length-1. For a stream where values arrive one at a time, a disjoint-set structure is the better fit: each new value creates a singleton and unions with its neighbours if present, keeping a running maximum of component sizes. That gives near-constant amortised updates and answers at any point, which the batch algorithm cannot do.

question: Contains duplicate: does the array have any duplicates?

followups.q: Which would you actually ship, the set or the sort?
followups.a: The set, in almost every case. It returns as soon as it finds a duplicate, which on real data with an early duplicate is dramatically faster than sorting the whole array, and it does not mutate the caller's input. Sorting wins when memory is genuinely tight, when the array is already sorted, or when the caller wanted it sorted anyway. The mutation point matters more than people expect: a predicate named `ContainsDuplicate` that reorders its argument is a nasty side effect to discover in production.

followups.q: What if the array is far too large to fit in memory?
followups.a: External sort and scan for adjacent equals is the exact answer. If an approximate answer is acceptable, a Bloom filter gives a large memory saving with a controllable false-positive rate, meaning it can wrongly report a duplicate but never miss one, so a positive can be confirmed with a second pass. Alternatively, partition by hash so equal values always land in the same partition, then check each partition independently in memory, which parallelises cleanly.

followups.q: What if you must find a duplicate in an array of n+1 integers in the range 1..n without modifying it and in O(1) space?
followups.a: That is a different problem with a much nicer solution: treat the values as `next` pointers, which by the pigeonhole principle must form a cycle, and run Floyd's tortoise and hare to find its entry. O(n) time, O(1) space, and the input is untouched. It is a favourite follow-up precisely because the hash-set instinct is useless there and the constraints are what point at the answer.

followups.q: Why presize the HashSet?
followups.a: A `HashSet<T>` grows by reallocating its bucket array and rehashing every element, so an unsized set filling with n items does about log n of those, each O(current size). Passing the capacity up front makes it one allocation. It does not change the asymptotic complexity, but it is measurable on large inputs and costs nothing to write, which makes it the sort of detail that reads as production experience rather than exam technique.

question: Insert Interval / Merge Intervals.

followups.q: Why Math.Max on the end rather than just taking the next interval's end?
followups.a: Because of nesting. If the current interval is [1,10] and the next is [2,3], the next one is entirely inside it, and assigning its end would shrink the merged interval to [1,3], silently losing coverage. Sorting by start does not guarantee the ends are ordered, so the maximum is required. It is the single most common bug in this problem and it only shows up on inputs containing a contained interval, which is exactly why that test case is there.

followups.q: Should [1,4] and [4,5] merge?
followups.a: It depends on whether the intervals are closed or half-open, and asking is the right move. For closed intervals sharing the endpoint 4, they overlap and merge to [1,5], which is what the code does with `<=`. For half-open intervals such as time slots, where [1,4) ends the instant [4,5) begins, they are adjacent but disjoint and the comparison should be `<`. Getting this wrong in a calendar system produces meetings that either falsely conflict or falsely do not.

followups.q: What is the general pattern behind interval problems?
followups.a: The sweep line: sort the endpoints, move through them in order, and maintain a running state. Merging keeps the current interval; counting overlaps increments on each start and decrements on each end, which is how meeting rooms II works; finding the maximum concurrency tracks the peak of that counter. Once you see a problem as events on a timeline rather than as pairs of numbers, the whole family reduces to choosing what to track during the sweep.

question: Non-overlapping intervals: minimum removals to make intervals non-overlapping.

followups.q: Why sort by end rather than by start?
followups.a: Because the greedy choice must leave as much room as possible for the remaining intervals, and the one that finishes earliest does exactly that. The last test case shows the failure of sorting by start: [0,10] comes first and, once kept, blocks all three short intervals, giving an answer of 3 removals when the optimum is 1. The exchange argument is that any optimal solution can be modified to include the earliest-finishing interval without getting worse, which is what makes the greedy provably correct.

followups.q: Why is touching not counted as overlapping here?
followups.a: Because [1,2] and [2,3] share only the instant 2, which under the half-open reading of intervals means they are adjacent rather than overlapping. That is why the comparison is `>=` rather than `>`. If the intervals were closed and sharing an endpoint counted as a conflict, the comparison would flip and the third test case would return 1 instead of 0. It is the same closed-versus-half-open question as in merge intervals and meeting rooms, and it must be settled from the problem statement rather than assumed.

followups.q: How does this relate to the minimum number of arrows to burst balloons?
followups.a: It is the same greedy with the comparison inverted. There you count how many groups of overlapping intervals exist, shooting one arrow per group, so you keep extending while intervals overlap rather than skipping them. Both sort by end and sweep once. Recognising that a family of interval problems reduces to sort-by-end-then-sweep, differing only in what is counted, is worth more than any individual solution.

question: Meeting rooms II: minimum meeting rooms required.

followups.q: Is it really valid to sort the start and end times separately, breaking the pairing?
followups.a: Yes, and it is the part worth justifying. The question is only how many meetings are active at a given moment, which depends on how many starts have occurred minus how many ends have. Which specific end belongs to which start never affects that count. So the two sorted sequences can be swept independently. It feels wrong at first glance, which is exactly why an interviewer asks, and being able to explain why it is sound is the answer they want.

followups.q: Why does ends[e] <= start free a room, rather than a strict less-than?
followups.a: Because a meeting ending at 10 and another starting at 10 can share a room, under the usual half-open interpretation of time slots. Using strict less-than would allocate a second room for back-to-back meetings, which is the third test case: it would return 2 instead of 1. If the convention were that a room needs turnover time, the comparison would change, which is another instance of the closed-versus-half-open decision that has to be made explicitly.

followups.q: How would you also report which meetings go in which room?
followups.a: Use the heap version and store the room index alongside the end time, so that when you reuse the earliest-finishing room you know its number, and when you allocate a new one you assign the next index. That gives a concrete schedule rather than just a count, which is what any real booking system actually needs. It is the same relationship as between computing a shortest path's length and recovering the path itself: one extra field, tracked as you go.

question: Find the kth largest element in an array.

followups.q: Why a min-heap for the kth LARGEST? It feels backwards.
followups.a: Because you want cheap access to the weakest member of the winning set, so it can be evicted when something better arrives. The heap holds the k largest seen so far, and its root is the smallest of those, which is precisely the kth largest overall. Using a max-heap would put the biggest element at the root, which you never need to evict, and you would have to hold all n elements to find the kth. The rule of thumb is that a bounded top-k needs a heap ordered opposite to the direction you are selecting.

followups.q: When is quickselect's O(n²) worst case a real problem?
followups.a: When the pivot is chosen deterministically, for example always the last element, and the input is sorted or adversarial: every partition removes one element and it degrades to quadratic. That is exploitable if inputs come from users, which is a genuine denial-of-service vector. Randomising the pivot, as above, makes the bad case vanishingly unlikely. The median-of-medians algorithm gives a guaranteed O(n) worst case but has constants bad enough that it is rarely used in practice.

followups.q: Which would you use for a continuous stream of values?
followups.a: The heap, because it handles unbounded input in O(k) memory and gives the answer at any moment. Quickselect needs the entire array materialised and reorders it, so it cannot apply. This is also why the heap approach generalises to top-k frequent elements, k closest points and the sliding-window problems, all of which are really 'maintain a bounded best set as data arrives'.

question: Top K frequent elements.

followups.q: Why can bucket sort beat the O(n log n) sorting lower bound here?
followups.a: Because that bound applies to comparison-based sorting, and bucket sort is not comparison-based. It exploits a structural fact about the data: frequencies are integers in the range 1 to n, so a value can be placed directly at its index rather than compared into position. Counting sort and radix sort do the same thing. Whenever keys are bounded small integers, the comparison lower bound simply does not apply, and noticing that is the real insight of this problem.

followups.q: How would you break ties, and is the output order defined?
followups.a: It is not defined here: elements with equal frequency come out in dictionary enumeration order, which .NET does not guarantee. If the problem needs deterministic output, such as 'ties broken alphabetically' in the top-k-words variant, you must sort within each bucket or use a comparer in the heap that compares frequency first and then the value. Tests that assert an exact order without specifying tie-breaking are a classic source of intermittent failures.

followups.q: What if the data does not fit on one machine?
followups.a: Count locally on each shard, then combine: since counts are additive, each shard sends its own top candidates plus their counts to a coordinator that sums and selects. The subtlety is that an element outside every shard's local top-k can still be globally top-k, so shards must send more than k, or you accept an approximation. The exact fix is a two-pass approach, and the approximate one is a Count-Min Sketch, which is how real streaming systems compute heavy hitters.

question: Decode ways: count how many ways to decode a digit string to letters (A=1..Z=26).

followups.q: Why is zero the hard part?
followups.a: Because it is the only digit with no single-character decoding, so it cannot stand alone and must be absorbed into a pair. That pair can only be 10 or 20, since 30 and above exceed Z. So "100" fails: the first zero pairs with the one to make 10, but the second zero has nothing valid before it. Most wrong solutions handle a leading zero and miss the interior case, which is why "100" and "301" are the test cases that matter.

followups.q: Why return 0 immediately when current hits zero?
followups.a: Because an undecodable position makes the whole string undecodable, and continuing would let later positions read a stale rolling value and produce a non-zero answer. It is also a genuine early exit rather than only a correctness guard. The alternative is to keep going with zeros propagating naturally, which also works if the recurrence is written carefully, but the explicit return states the intent and avoids relying on zero-multiplication behaviour.

followups.q: Suppose the alphabet were larger, say 1 to 100.
followups.a: The recurrence generalises to looking back up to three digits, with the validity test becoming a range check on one, two and three-digit numbers. The structure is unchanged: sum the ways from each position that can reach here by a valid token. That is the general 'count the tokenisations' shape, and it is the same DP that underlies counting the ways to segment a string, which is why word break and decode ways feel related despite looking different.

question: Sliding window maximum: max in each window of size k.

followups.q: Why store indices rather than values in the deque?
followups.a: Because the window's left boundary is expressed in index terms, and without indices you cannot tell whether the front element has expired. Values alone would leave you unable to distinguish a maximum still inside the window from one that slid out, especially with duplicates. Storing indices also makes the value lookup trivial, since `nums[index]` is always available. It is a small decision that makes the expiry check O(1) rather than impossible.

followups.q: Why pop with <= rather than <, and does it matter for duplicates?
followups.a: Either works for correctness of the maximum, but `<=` keeps the deque smaller by evicting equal values, which is fine because the later duplicate survives at least as long as the earlier one. Using `<` would retain both, which costs memory but still yields the right answer since the front is the same value either way. The `[7,7,7]` test exercises this; if the expiry check were wrong, the retained-duplicate version would expose it sooner, which is a mild argument for keeping `<`.

followups.q: Suppose you needed the median of each window rather than the maximum.
followups.a: The deque trick does not apply, because a median needs order statistics rather than a single extreme, and there is no way to discard elements as permanently useless. The standard approach is two heaps, a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper, with lazy deletion of expired indices, giving O(n log k). An order-statistic tree or an indexed skip list is the cleaner alternative. It is a good illustration that a small change in the aggregate can change the required data structure entirely.

question: Plus one: increment a number represented as a digit array.

followups.q: Why is the all-nines case worth special handling rather than a general carry loop?
followups.a: Because it is the only case where the result has more digits than the input, so it is the only one that needs a new allocation. Every other case mutates in place and returns early. Handling it after the loop keeps the hot path allocation-free, and relying on a freshly allocated int array defaulting to zero means only the leading 1 has to be written. Candidates who forget it return 000 for 999, which is a very visible failure.

followups.q: The method mutates its input. Is that acceptable?
followups.a: It is what the standard problem expects, but it is a genuine side effect: the caller's array is modified even in the cases where a new array is returned, since the nines were already zeroed. That inconsistency is the worst part, because the behaviour differs depending on the data. In production I would either always copy, or name the method to make the mutation obvious, or return void and document that the array is updated in place when it can be.

followups.q: Why represent a number as a digit array at all?
followups.a: Because it is not bounded by any built-in type, which is the whole point: a thousand-digit number has no int or long representation. This is the same reason the add-two-numbers linked list problem exists. Real big-number libraries such as BigInteger use the same idea but pack several digits into each element, typically working in base 2^32, so the carry logic is identical while the storage is far more compact.

question: Next permutation: rearrange to the next lexicographically greater permutation.

followups.q: Why reverse the suffix rather than sort it?
followups.a: Because the suffix is guaranteed non-increasing by the way the pivot was found, and after the swap it remains non-increasing, so reversing it produces exactly the ascending order that sorting would, in O(n) instead of O(n log n). Sorting would give the same answer and is not wrong, just unnecessarily slow, and reaching for it suggests you have not noticed the invariant that makes the algorithm linear. Stating why the suffix is already ordered is the substance of the answer.

followups.q: Why does scanning from the right find the SMALLEST element greater than the pivot?
followups.a: Because the suffix is non-increasing, so values get smaller as you move right. The first element from the right that exceeds the pivot is therefore the smallest such element in the suffix. Swapping with anything larger would skip permutations and give a later one rather than the immediate next. It is a one-line detail that decides between 'a greater permutation' and 'the next greater permutation'.

followups.q: Where is this used outside interviews?
followups.a: It is the standard way to enumerate permutations lazily, one at a time, in constant extra space, which matters when the full set is too large to materialise. C++ exposes it directly as std::next_permutation and .NET has no equivalent, so it is worth knowing. Repeatedly applying it from the sorted array visits every permutation exactly once in lexicographic order and returns to the start, which the [3,2,1] wrap case demonstrates.

question: Sort colors (Dutch national flag): sort an array of 0s, 1s, 2s in one pass.

followups.q: Why is mid advanced after swapping a 0 but not after swapping a 2?
followups.a: Because of where the incoming value came from. When a 0 is swapped to `low`, the value that arrives at `mid` came from the region below `mid`, which has already been scanned and can only be a 1, so it is safe to move on. When a 2 is swapped to `high`, the arriving value came from beyond `high`, which has never been examined and could be anything, so `mid` must stay and re-inspect it. Advancing in both cases is the classic bug and produces an array that is almost sorted, which is exactly the sort of error that slips through casual testing.

followups.q: Why mid <= high rather than mid < high?
followups.a: Because when `mid` and `high` coincide there is still one unexamined element at that position. Stopping early leaves it unsorted, which shows up on short inputs such as [1,0]. It is the standard inclusive-bound question, and the way to settle it is to ask what the pointers mean: `high` is the first settled 2, so everything strictly below it including `mid` still needs classifying.

followups.q: Why not just count the three values and rewrite the array?
followups.a: Counting sort in two passes is simpler, equally O(n), and often faster in practice. The one-pass constraint exists because the real problem is partitioning around a pivot with three-way handling of equal elements, which is exactly what quicksort needs to avoid quadratic behaviour on arrays with many duplicates. So the value of this exercise is the partitioning technique, not the sorting of three specific values. That is also why it is called the Dutch national flag problem, after Dijkstra.

question: Palindrome partitioning: return all palindrome substring partitions.

followups.q: Why does the palindrome DP loop start from the end and work backwards?
followups.a: Because `isPalindrome[start, end]` depends on `isPalindrome[start+1, end-1]`, a shorter substring starting one later. Iterating `start` downwards guarantees that inner value is already computed. Getting the loop order wrong here reads uninitialised entries, which default to false, so the code silently misses palindromes rather than crashing. Whenever a DP recurrence refers to a larger index, the loop over that index has to run in the opposite direction.
