followups.q: Suppose you only need the minimum number of cuts, not every partition.
followups.a: That is Palindrome Partitioning II, and it becomes a one-dimensional DP rather than an enumeration: `cuts[i]` is the fewest cuts for the first i characters, computed as the best over every j where the substring j..i is a palindrome. That is O(n^2) total, against exponential for listing all partitions. The distinction is worth stating explicitly, because the number of partitions can be exponential, so any problem asking for all of them cannot be polynomial no matter how clever the algorithm.

followups.q: Is the precomputed table actually worth it here?
followups.a: It does not change the exponential output bound, but it removes an O(n) factor from every node of the recursion tree, which is a real constant-factor win on longer strings. It costs O(n^2) memory, which for a string of a few thousand characters is fine and for a very long one is not. If memory were the binding constraint, expanding around centres on demand and caching only recent results would be the compromise. Worth mentioning that the optimisation targets the per-node cost, not the tree size.

question: Gas station: find the starting index to complete a circular route.

followups.q: Why can every station between a failed start and the failure point be skipped?
followups.a: Because the tank was non-negative at every step from the candidate start up to just before the failure, so any later station in that range would begin its own journey with no more fuel than the original start had at that point, and would run out no later. Formally, if the partial sum from start to i is negative while all intermediate partial sums were non-negative, then every suffix of that range also sums negative. That is what turns an O(n^2) check of every start into a single pass.

followups.q: Why does a non-negative total guarantee a solution exists?
followups.a: Because the circuit is closed, so the sum of all surpluses is the fuel available for the whole loop. If it is non-negative, there must be some rotation of the sequence whose every prefix sum is non-negative, which is a standard result about cyclic sequences. The algorithm's final candidate is exactly that rotation. Without the total check you would return a start index even when the route is impossible, which is why the two pieces of bookkeeping are both necessary.

followups.q: Is the answer unique?
followups.a: Yes, when the total surplus is positive there is exactly one valid starting station. If the total is exactly zero the route is completable with the tank reaching zero at the end, and the start is still unique. That uniqueness is worth knowing because it means a test can assert an exact index without being fragile, unlike find-peak or reorganize-string where multiple answers are valid.

question: First missing positive integer in O(n) time and O(1) space.

followups.q: Why compare nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i] rather than checking the index directly?
followups.a: Because comparing values rather than positions terminates correctly on duplicates. With [1,1], the second 1 wants index 0, which already holds a 1, so the values match and the loop stops. A condition written as `nums[i] != i + 1` would keep swapping the two 1s forever, since neither is ever satisfied. That infinite loop on duplicate input is the most common failure of this algorithm and the reason the [1,1] test is there.

followups.q: Why is this O(n) when there is a while loop inside a for loop?
followups.a: Because every successful swap places at least one value at its permanent home, and a value at home is never moved again. So there can be at most n successful swaps in total across the entire run, regardless of how they cluster within the outer loop. The failed comparisons are bounded by n as well. It is the same amortised argument as for monotonic stacks: count the total work over the whole algorithm rather than per iteration.

followups.q: Why must the answer be between 1 and n+1?
followups.a: By the pigeonhole principle: with n slots you can hold at most n distinct values, so if 1 through n are all present the first missing is n+1, and if any of them is absent the answer is at most n. That bound is what makes the array usable as its own hash table, since every value worth tracking has a home index within it. Values outside the range are simply ignored, which is why negatives and large numbers need no special handling.

followups.q: Suppose the array must not be modified.
followups.a: Then the O(1) space bound is unreachable by this method and you need O(n) auxiliary space, either a hash set of the positives present or a boolean array of size n+1, scanned afterwards. That is simpler to write and usually what I would ship, since mutating the caller's array to answer a read-only question is a real side effect. The in-place version earns its place only when memory is genuinely constrained and the caller has agreed the input is disposable.

question: Word break: can a string be segmented into dictionary words?

followups.q: Why does greedy longest-match fail?
followups.a: Because an early choice can strand the remainder. In "catsandog" the longest first match is "cats", which leaves "andog" unsplittable, while "cat" would leave "sandog"; neither works here, but the same shape with "catsanddog" succeeds only via the shorter first word. Greedy has no way to undo a choice, so it needs the property that a locally longest match is always part of a solution, which segmentation does not have. That is what forces either backtracking or DP.

followups.q: What does the longest-word bound actually save?
followups.a: It caps the inner loop at the length of the longest dictionary word rather than the whole prefix, turning O(n²) substring attempts into O(n·L). For a realistic dictionary where words are short and the input is long, that is a large constant-factor win and sometimes an asymptotic one. It costs one pass over the dictionary to compute. A trie does the same job more elegantly, walking character by character and stopping the moment no word continues with that prefix.

followups.q: Suppose you must return all possible sentences, not just whether one exists.
followups.a: That is Word Break II, and the complexity changes fundamentally: the number of valid sentences can be exponential, so no polynomial algorithm exists for producing all of them. The practical approach is memoised recursion returning the list of sentences for each suffix, which avoids recomputing shared work but still pays for the output size. The important move is to run the boolean DP first as a feasibility check, so that hopeless inputs are rejected in polynomial time before the exponential enumeration starts.

question: Find peak element (any local maximum) in O(log n).

followups.q: How can binary search work on an unsorted array?
followups.a: Because the invariant is not sortedness but the existence of a peak within the current range. If the midpoint is lower than its right neighbour, the sequence ascends there, and since the array is bounded by negative infinity at the end, it must turn downward at some point on that side, so a peak exists to the right. The same argument mirrors leftwards. Binary search needs a decidable direction, not a total order, and that is a genuinely useful thing to internalise because it unlocks the whole 'binary search on the answer' family.

followups.q: The answer is not unique. How would you test this?
followups.a: Not by asserting a fixed index, which is what the second test case demonstrates: [1,2,1,3,5,6,4] has peaks at index 1 and index 5, and either is correct. The right assertion is a property check that the returned index really is greater than its existing neighbours. Tests that pin down one valid answer among many are fragile and break when an implementation detail changes, which is a point worth making whenever a problem admits multiple correct outputs.

followups.q: Suppose the array were two-dimensional and you needed a 2D peak.
followups.a: The same idea extends, but on columns rather than elements. Binary search the middle column, find its maximum element, and compare with the horizontal neighbours; move to whichever side is larger, because a peak must exist in that half by the same ascending argument. That gives O(rows log cols). The naive extension of comparing single elements does not work, which is why the column maximum is the necessary step and the usual sticking point.

question: Two Sum II (sorted input): return the two indices.

followups.q: Why is moving only one pointer at a time guaranteed not to miss the answer?
followups.a: Because of the sorted order. If the sum is too small, the current left element paired with anything to the left of right is even smaller, so left can never be part of a solution with any remaining partner and is safely discarded. The mirror argument applies when the sum is too large. Each step therefore eliminates exactly one element that provably cannot participate, which is why a single sweep suffices. That is the same exchange argument as in container-with-most-water.

followups.q: How does this differ from the unsorted Two Sum?
followups.a: The unsorted version needs a hash map, giving O(n) time and O(n) space, because there is no ordering to exploit. Here the sort has already been paid for, so two pointers give O(1) space. If the input were unsorted and you sorted it yourself, you would pay O(n log n) and lose the original indices, which is why the hash map remains the right answer there. The lesson is that a precondition in the problem statement often points directly at the intended algorithm.

followups.q: Why 1-based indices, and how would you handle that in real code?
followups.a: It is a convention this particular problem specifies, and it is the sort of detail that causes silent off-by-one bugs when carried between problems. In production I would return 0-based indices to match every other .NET API, or return the values rather than the indices if that is what the caller needs. Where a 1-based contract is imposed by an external system, I would convert at the boundary and keep the internal code 0-based, rather than letting the foreign convention leak inward.

question: Check if a string has all unique characters without extra data structures.
answer: If limited to ASCII/lowercase, use a bit vector (an int as a bitmask): for each char, check/set its bit; a repeated bit means a duplicate. O(n) time, O(1) space. With a boolean array of 128/256 it's also O(1) space. Sorting in place is O(n log n) if no extra structure allowed.

question: Maximum number of consecutive ones III (flip at most k zeros).

followups.q: Why does the left pointer never move backwards, and why does that matter?
followups.a: Because a window that was invalid at some left position can only become valid by shrinking, never by growing, so there is no reason to revisit an earlier left. Both pointers therefore advance monotonically, and each index is visited at most twice across the whole run, which is what makes the nested loop linear rather than quadratic. Whenever you see a while loop inside a for loop in a sliding window, that monotonic argument is the thing to state, because otherwise the complexity looks like O(n^2).

followups.q: Suppose you also needed to return the actual window, or which zeros to flip.
followups.a: Record the left index whenever the best improves, which gives the window's bounds directly; the zeros to flip are then simply the zero positions inside it, findable in one pass over that range. It costs one extra integer. The same pattern applies across this family: the algorithm naturally computes a length, and recovering the witness needs only the start index saved at the moment of improvement.

followups.q: Suppose flipping a zero had a cost that varied by position, with a total budget.
followups.a: The counter becomes a running sum of costs rather than a count, and the shrink condition compares that sum against the budget. That still works because costs are non-negative, so the sum is monotonic in the window and the shrink rule remains valid. If costs could be negative the monotonicity breaks and sliding windows stop applying, exactly as they do for subarray sums with negative numbers, where prefix sums with a hash map take over.

question: First unique character in a string.

followups.q: Why not iterate the dictionary looking for the first count of 1?
followups.a: Because dictionary order is not the string's order. .NET makes no guarantee about `Dictionary<K,V>` enumeration order, and although it often looks like insertion order in practice, that is an implementation detail that has changed between versions and breaks as soon as a removal occurs. The character that enumerates first may not be the one that appears first in the string, so the answer would be wrong for reasons that are invisible in testing. Scanning the string is both correct and obviously correct.

followups.q: What if characters arrive as a stream and you must answer at any moment?
followups.a: Keep a queue of candidate characters alongside the counts. On each arrival, increment its count and push it onto the queue, then pop from the front while the front element's count exceeds one. The queue head is then always the current first-unique, answered in O(1) amortised. That is the standard 'first non-repeating character in a stream' problem, and the queue is what turns a two-pass algorithm into an online one.

followups.q: Would an int[26] be better here?
followups.a: If the input is guaranteed lowercase ASCII, yes: no hashing, no allocation beyond a tiny array, and far better cache behaviour. The cost is that it silently breaks on any other input, since `c - 'a'` goes negative for an uppercase letter and either throws or corrupts memory in unchecked contexts. Use it when the constraint is stated, and say that you are relying on it, rather than quietly assuming the alphabet.

question: Reverse a singly linked list.

followups.q: Write the recursive version, and say when you would not use it.
followups.a: Recurse to the end to get the new head, then on the way back out set `head.Next.Next = head` and `head.Next = null`, returning the new head unchanged through every frame. It is four lines and reads beautifully. You would not use it when the list length is unbounded or attacker-influenced, because .NET does not eliminate tail calls reliably and a list of a million nodes will overflow the stack. Rule of thumb: recursion is fine on trees, where depth is logarithmic if balanced, and risky on lists, where depth is the full length.

followups.q: How would you reverse only a section, from position m to n?
followups.a: Walk to the node before position m and keep it as an anchor, reverse the sublist with the same three-pointer loop while counting to n, then reconnect: the anchor points at the new sub-head, and the old sub-head, which is now the sub-tail, points at the remainder. Use a dummy node before the head so that m equal to 1 needs no special case, which is the usual source of bugs here. Still one pass and O(1) space.

followups.q: Why does this need a singly linked list at all, when List<T> exists?
followups.a: In application code it usually does not, and `List<T>` with `Reverse` is the right answer. The structure earns its keep when you need O(1) insertion or removal given a node reference and never need indexing, which is exactly why `LinkedList<T>` underpins an LRU cache. The interview value of the question is different: it tests whether you can manipulate references without losing the list, which is the same skill as not corrupting state in any pointer-like structure.

question: Detect a cycle in a linked list.

followups.q: Why does resetting to the head find the cycle entry? Prove it.
followups.a: Let the distance from head to the cycle entry be `a`, from the entry to the meeting point be `b`, and the remainder of the cycle be `c`. When they meet, slow has travelled `a + b` and fast `a + b + k(b + c)` for some number of laps k, and fast has travelled exactly twice as far. Solving gives `a = c + (k-1)(b+c)`, meaning the distance from the head to the entry equals the distance from the meeting point to the entry, modulo whole laps. So two pointers advancing one step each from the head and from the meeting point arrive at the entry together.

followups.q: Why two steps for the fast pointer rather than three?
followups.a: Correctness only needs the gap to close by a whole number of positions per step, and larger strides still work, but a stride of two guarantees the fast pointer cannot jump over the slow one, since it gains exactly one position per iteration. With a stride of three it gains two, and in a cycle whose length shares a factor with that gain the pointers can leapfrog for longer before coinciding. Two is also the stride for which the entry-point proof above comes out clean, which is why it is the canonical choice.

followups.q: Where does this pattern show up outside linked lists?
followups.a: Any iterated function where you follow `x = f(x)` and need to detect that it repeats without storing history. Cycle detection in a functional graph, Pollard's rho for integer factorisation, detecting a repeating state in a pseudo-random generator, and finding the repeating part of a decimal expansion all use it. The Happy Number problem is the same algorithm applied to digit-square sums, which is why an interviewer may follow this question with that one.

followups.q: Why ReferenceEquals rather than ==?
followups.a: For a plain class with no operator overload they are identical, so it is a readability choice here: it states that identity, not value, is what matters. It stops being a stylistic point if the node type ever overloads `==` or `Equals` to compare values, at which point `==` could report true for two distinct nodes holding the same value and the detection would be wrong. `ReferenceEquals` cannot be overridden, so it is immune to that.

question: Find the middle of a linked list.

followups.q: Why not just count the nodes and walk half way?
followups.a: It works and is O(n) either way, but it needs two passes over the list. That is irrelevant for an in-memory list and important when the list is a stream you can only read once, or when each traversal has real cost such as following pointers across pages. The two-pointer version also composes: the same slow and fast walk detects a cycle, finds the nth node from the end, and splits a list for merge sort, so it is the technique worth having in your hands.

followups.q: Which middle should you return, and does it matter?
followups.a: It matters a great deal for merge sort. If you split at the second middle, a two-node list splits into an empty half and a two-node half, so the recursion never shrinks and you get infinite recursion. Splitting at the first middle guarantees both halves are strictly smaller. For a plain 'find the middle' API either is fine as long as it is documented, but the merge sort case is the concrete reason the distinction exists.

followups.q: What if the list has a cycle?
followups.a: The loop never terminates, because the fast pointer never reaches null. If a cycle is possible you have to detect it first with the same slow and fast walk, since 'the middle' of a cyclic list is not a well-defined concept anyway. In practice this is why library code that walks user-supplied linked structures either guarantees acyclicity by construction or carries an explicit visited check, rather than assuming a well-formed input.

question: Merge two sorted linked lists.

followups.q: Now merge k sorted lists.
followups.a: Two good answers. A min-heap holding the current head of each list gives O(N log k) for N total nodes: pop the smallest, append it, push its successor. Or merge pairwise in rounds, halving the number of lists each round, which is the same O(N log k) and needs no heap. Both beat the naive approach of merging one list into an accumulator at a time, which is O(Nk) because the accumulator is re-walked on every merge, and that difference is the point of the follow-up.

followups.q: Why a dummy node rather than handling the first element specially?
followups.a: Because without it every append must ask whether the result is still empty, which means a branch inside the hot loop and a separate variable for the head. The dummy makes the first append identical to every other one, then `dummy.Next` is the real head. The same technique removes edge cases whenever the head of a list might change: removing the nth node from the end, deleting by value, reversing a sublist from position 1. It costs one node that is discarded on return.

followups.q: What if the lists are arrays instead?
followups.a: The same two-pointer merge, but it needs an output array of size n + m because you cannot relink; that extra allocation is the real difference between merging lists and merging arrays, and it is why merge sort on an array is not in-place while merge sort on a list can be. The .NET variant of this question is usually the in-place one where the first array already has trailing space, and the trick there is to fill from the back, so that writing never overwrites an element still to be read.

question: Remove the nth node from the end of a linked list.

followups.q: What exactly does the dummy node buy you here?
followups.a: Without it, deleting the head is a different operation from deleting any other node: you must return `head.Next` rather than relink a predecessor, so the code needs a branch and a separate return path. With the dummy, the head has a predecessor like everything else, so there is exactly one deletion path and one return statement. The same trick applies to any list operation where the head might change, and it removes the single most common source of null-reference bugs in these problems.

followups.q: How should an out-of-range n behave?
followups.a: Silently returning the list unchanged, as above, is one choice; throwing ArgumentOutOfRangeException is another. What matters is deciding deliberately and documenting it, because the two lead to very different debugging experiences. My preference in library code is to throw, since a caller asking for the fifth-from-last node of a two-element list has a bug and a silent no-op hides it. For a forgiving API, returning unchanged is defensible.

followups.q: Could you delete a node given only a reference to it, with no access to the head?
followups.a: Yes, with a trick: copy the next node's value into the current node, then unlink the next node. You are not really deleting the given node, you are making it impersonate its successor. It fails for the tail, since there is no successor to copy from, and it is invisible to any other reference to that specific node, which will now see a different value. That caveat is the point of the question, and mentioning it is what separates a real answer from a memorised one.

question: Add two numbers represented as linked lists (digits reversed).

followups.q: What changes if the digits are stored most-significant first?
followups.a: The alignment breaks, because addition proceeds from the least significant end and you can no longer walk forward in step. Three options: reverse both lists, add, then reverse the result; push both onto stacks and pop to get least-significant-first order; or recurse to the end after padding the shorter list and carry back up the return path. The stack version is usually cleanest and does not mutate the inputs, which matters if the caller still needs them.

followups.q: Why is carry part of the loop condition rather than handled after the loop?
followups.a: Because handling it afterwards means a duplicated node-append and an easily forgotten branch, and forgetting it is exactly why 5 + 5 returns 0 instead of 10 in many first attempts. Folding it into the condition makes the final carry just another iteration with both lists exhausted. The same structure handles all three ragged cases uniformly: one list longer, the other longer, or a carry outliving both.

followups.q: Why use a linked list at all rather than parsing to a number?
followups.a: Because the representation exists to handle numbers larger than any built-in type. Converting to long works for short lists and overflows silently beyond nineteen digits, which is precisely the case the data structure is designed for. This is a miniature bignum implementation, and the same digit-by-digit-with-carry logic underpins BigInteger, with the real version storing several digits per element for efficiency rather than one.

question: Reorder a linked list (L0→Ln→L1→Ln-1→...).

followups.q: Why split at the first middle rather than the second?
followups.a: Because it guarantees the second half is no longer than the first, which makes the interleaving loop terminate naturally when the reversed half runs out, leaving the first half's final node at the end. Splitting at the second middle would make the second half longer on even-length lists, and the loop would need an extra guard to avoid attaching a stray node twice. It is the same distinction that matters when splitting for merge sort, where the wrong middle causes infinite recursion.

followups.q: Why detach the halves with slow.Next = null?
followups.a: Because without it the first half still points into the second, which is now reversed, creating a cycle: following the list would loop forever. The detachment is one line and its absence produces a hang rather than a wrong answer, which is much harder to diagnose. It is the same class of omission as forgetting to null the tail when merging k sorted lists, and both are worth checking explicitly whenever you rewire list pointers.

followups.q: Could you do it with an array instead?
followups.a: Yes, and it is far simpler: copy the nodes into a list, then walk two pointers from both ends rewiring as you go. That is O(n) time and O(n) space. The pointer version exists to meet the O(1) space constraint, and it is worth saying that if the constraint were absent, the array version is the one I would ship for readability. Naming the trade-off rather than assuming the clever version is always wanted is usually the better answer.

question: Check if a linked list is a palindrome.

followups.q: Is mutating the list to answer a read-only question acceptable?
followups.a: Only if you restore it, as here, and even then it is not thread-safe: another thread reading the list during the check sees it half-reversed, and an exception thrown mid-comparison would leave it broken permanently. If the structure is shared or the code must be reentrant, the O(n) copy is the correct choice and the space is the price of safety. Being able to name that trade-off rather than reflexively optimising for space is the better answer.

followups.q: Why compare using the second half as the loop driver?
followups.a: Because on an odd-length list the halves differ by one node, and the middle element has no partner and never needs comparing. Driving the loop from the shorter second half makes that automatic, with no length bookkeeping and no separate odd and even cases. Driving it from the first half instead would run one step past the end of the second and dereference null, which is the standard bug in this problem.

followups.q: How would you do it recursively in O(n) time?
followups.a: Recurse to the end while keeping a front pointer in an outer variable; as each frame returns, compare the front pointer's value to the current node's and advance the front pointer. It is elegant and uses O(n) stack space, which on a long list risks the same stack overflow as any deep list recursion. It is a good thing to mention as an alternative, and a bad thing to actually ship for lists whose length you do not control.

question: Find the intersection node of two singly linked lists.

followups.q: Why does switching heads make the pointers meet?
followups.a: Let the unique prefixes be lengths m and n and the shared tail be length c. The first pointer travels m + c to the end of list A, then n to reach the intersection from list B's head, for m + c + n in total. The second travels n + c + m. Those are equal, so both arrive at the intersection after the same number of steps. When there is no shared tail, both traverse m + n and hit null simultaneously, which is why the null case needs no special handling.

followups.q: Why compare node identity rather than values?
followups.a: Because intersection means the lists share the same physical node from some point on, not that they happen to contain equal values. The third test case has two lists with identical values 1 and 2 that never intersect, and a value-based comparison would wrongly report a meeting at the first node. `ReferenceEquals` states that identity is what matters and is immune to any `==` overload the node type might acquire later.

followups.q: What are the alternatives, and why is this preferred?
followups.a: You can measure both lengths, advance the longer list by the difference, then walk together, which is also O(m + n) and O(1) but needs two extra passes and explicit arithmetic. Or store one list's nodes in a hash set and scan the other, which is O(m + n) time but O(m) space. The two-pointer switch is preferred because it needs no length computation, no extra memory and no special cases. The same technique solves finding the lowest common ancestor when nodes have parent pointers, which is the same problem in a tree.

question: Copy a linked list with random pointers.

followups.q: Why can't a single forward pass resolve the random pointers?
followups.a: Because a random pointer can target a node later in the list that has not been cloned yet, so there is nothing to point at. The dictionary solves it by creating every clone first and wiring afterwards; the weaving trick solves it by making the clone's location derivable from the original's, so the clone exists implicitly as soon as the original is reachable. Both are answers to the same ordering problem, and it is the same forward-reference issue that clone-graph solves by registering the clone before recursing.

followups.q: Why unweave at the end rather than leaving the lists interleaved?
followups.a: Because the caller still holds a reference to the original head and expects an unmodified list. Leaving it interleaved would double its apparent length and interleave foreign nodes into it, which is a severe side effect for a method named Copy. The unweaving pass is also where a partly-written implementation usually goes wrong, since both lists must be rebuilt simultaneously and the null handling at the tail is easy to get wrong.

followups.q: Which would you ship?
followups.a: The dictionary version, in almost every case. It is a third of the length, obviously correct on inspection, and does not mutate the input even temporarily, so it is safe if another thread is reading the list. The weaving version is a genuine O(1)-space improvement and worth knowing, but the space saved is proportional to the list you are already duplicating, so the ceiling on the benefit is a factor of two. That is rarely worth the readability and the transient corruption.

question: Merge k sorted linked lists.

followups.q: Why is merging one at a time O(Nk) rather than O(N log k)?
followups.a: Because the accumulated list is traversed again on every merge. After merging j lists the accumulator holds roughly jN/k nodes, and merging the next list walks all of them, so the total is the sum over j, which is quadratic in k. Pairwise halving avoids it because each round touches every node exactly once and there are only log k rounds. It is the same reason building a string by repeated concatenation in a loop is quadratic while a StringBuilder is linear.

followups.q: Why set tail.Next = null at the end of the heap version?
followups.a: Because the final node appended still carries its original `Next` pointer into whatever followed it in its own list. Those nodes were already consumed and appended elsewhere, so leaving the pointer creates a stale link, and in the worst case a cycle that makes the result list infinite. Nulling the tail is one line and the kind of omission that produces a hang rather than a clean failure, which is far harder to diagnose.

followups.q: Which would you ship?
followups.a: Pairwise, usually. It has no heap allocation, no comparer indirection, and excellent memory locality, and in practice it tends to beat the heap version despite identical asymptotics. The heap wins when the lists arrive as streams of unknown length or when k is large and you cannot hold all the heads at once, and it is the version that generalises to an external merge over files, which is how database sort-merge joins and log-structured merge trees work.

question: Reverse nodes in k-group.

followups.q: Why check for a full group before reversing rather than reversing and fixing up?
followups.a: Because the problem requires a trailing partial group to keep its original order, and once you have reversed a partial group, restoring it costs another reversal. Checking first is a cheap k-step walk and makes the main loop unconditional. The alternative some people write, counting the whole list up front and dividing, also works but needs an extra full traversal and an index to track, which is more state to get wrong.

followups.q: Why does groupStart become the group's tail?
followups.a: Because reversal turns the first node into the last. Capturing it before the reversal gives you the node that will need to point at whatever follows the group, which is the `next` pointer left over from the reversal loop. Missing that reconnection is the classic failure: the reversed group becomes an isolated fragment and the rest of the list is lost, which shows up as truncated output rather than an exception.

followups.q: How would you do this recursively, and would you?
followups.a: Reverse the first k nodes, then recurse on the remainder and attach the result to the group's tail. It is noticeably shorter and reads well. I would not ship it, because the recursion depth is the list length divided by k, so a long list with a small k overflows the stack, and .NET cannot catch that. It is the same reasoning as for reversing a whole list: recursion is fine on balanced trees, risky on lists whose length you do not control.

question: Remove duplicates from a sorted linked list.

followups.q: Why not advance current after skipping a duplicate?
followups.a: Because the new successor might also be a duplicate. With three 1s, skipping once leaves the current node pointing at the second 1; advancing immediately would move past it and leave the duplicate in place. Staying put re-examines the new successor and collapses the whole run. The test with [1,1,1] exists precisely to catch that, since a version that advances unconditionally passes on pairs and fails on triples.

followups.q: Why does the remove-all variant need a dummy head when the first does not?
followups.a: Because it can delete the head itself, as when the list starts with a run of duplicates, so the returned head differs from the one passed in. The dummy gives the head a predecessor like every other node, so the splice logic has one code path and the answer is simply `dummy.Next`. The keep-one variant never deletes the head, since the first occurrence of any value survives, so it can return the original head unchanged.

followups.q: Suppose the list were not sorted.
followups.a: Adjacency no longer implies equality, so you need a hash set of seen values and a single pass splicing out anything already present, giving O(n) time and O(n) space. Without extra space it degrades to O(n^2) with a nested scan per node. That contrast is the point worth making: sorting is what buys the O(1) space here, so if the caller can guarantee sorted input it is worth relying on, and if not the space cost is unavoidable.

question: Rotate a linked list to the right by k places.

followups.q: Why form a ring rather than just finding the split point directly?
followups.a: Because the new head and the old tail need connecting anyway, and closing the ring does that before you know where the cut goes. Without it you would hold three pointers, the old tail, the new tail and the new head, and wire them in the right order afterwards. The ring makes the operation a single cut, which is both fewer steps and harder to get wrong. The one hazard is that the list is temporarily cyclic, so an exception thrown between closing and cutting would leave it corrupted.

followups.q: Why is k % length necessary rather than just an optimisation?
followups.a: Because without it the walk `length - k` goes negative for k greater than the length, so the loop either does nothing or runs past the end depending on how it is written, producing a wrong answer or a null dereference. The [1] rotated by 99 test would fail immediately. It is the same reduction as in array rotation, and as there, if k could be negative you would need the double-modulo idiom to bring it into range.

followups.q: How does this compare with rotating an array?
followups.a: The array version cannot relink, so it uses three reversals or cyclic replacement, both O(n) time and O(1) space but performing O(n) writes. The list version performs exactly two pointer writes after the traversal, because relinking is O(1) once you have found the position. That is one of the few places a linked list genuinely beats an array, and it is worth naming since most comparisons go the other way.

question: Swap nodes in pairs.

followups.q: Why not just swap the values, which is far simpler?
followups.a: Because the problem asks for the nodes to be swapped, and in real structures the distinction matters: other code may hold references to specific nodes and expect them to stay put relative to their data, or the payload may be large enough that copying is expensive. In an interview, swapping values is usually treated as sidestepping the exercise, since the whole point is to test careful pointer manipulation. It is worth stating that you know the shortcut exists and why you are not taking it.

followups.q: This is reverse-k-group with k = 2. Would you just call that?
followups.a: You could, and it would be correct. In production, one general method beats two special ones, so reusing it is the right call. The specialised version here is shorter and has no reversal loop, so it is marginally faster and much easier to verify by eye. The general guidance is to prefer the general method unless the specialisation is on a hot path, and the fact that the two are related is worth saying out loud since interviewers often ask them in sequence.

followups.q: Why advance prev to first rather than to second?
followups.a: Because after the swap, first is the pair's tail: the order is second then first, so first is what must point at the next pair. Advancing to second would leave prev pointing at the pair's head and the following pair would be wired into the wrong place, producing a list that loses nodes or loops. Tracing a four-node list by hand is the quickest way to convince yourself, and it is the step most often gotten backwards.

question: Implement a stack using two queues (or a queue using two stacks).

followups.q: Why is the two-stack queue amortised O(1) when a single dequeue can cost O(n)?
followups.a: Because each element is moved from the inbox to the outbox exactly once in its lifetime. A transfer that moves n elements has effectively paid for the next n dequeues, which are then O(1) each. Summing over any sequence of operations, the total work is linear in the number of elements, so the average per operation is constant. It is the same accounting argument as for a dynamic array's doubling growth, and it is why amortised analysis matters rather than looking only at the worst single call.

followups.q: Why refill only when the outbox is empty, rather than after each dequeue?
followups.a: Because refilling eagerly would move elements back and forth repeatedly and destroy the amortised bound, turning it into O(n) per operation. The empty check is the entire optimisation. It also preserves correctness: elements already in the outbox are older than anything in the inbox, so pushing new arrivals on top of them would break the FIFO order. The test case that enqueues 4 while the outbox still holds items is there to catch exactly that mistake.

followups.q: Why would anyone do this in practice?
followups.a: Rarely for the data structures themselves, since both are built in. The pattern is genuinely useful though: the inbox-outbox split is how you batch expensive operations, for instance accumulating writes and flushing them in one transaction, or buffering log lines and shipping them in blocks. Persistent functional queues use exactly this two-list structure because it gives amortised O(1) with immutable lists. So the value is the amortisation technique rather than the queue.

question: Min stack: stack with O(1) getMin.

followups.q: Can you avoid the O(n) extra space?
followups.a: Partly. One approach stores encoded values: when a new minimum arrives, push `2*value - currentMin`, which is below the new minimum and can be decoded on pop to recover the previous one. It reaches O(1) extra space but risks overflow and is genuinely hard to read. The gentler optimisation is to push onto the minimum stack only when the value is less than or equal to the current minimum, and pop only when the popped value equals the top: that keeps it O(1) amortised for typical data while staying obvious. The `equal to` in both conditions is essential, as the duplicate test above shows.

followups.q: How would you make it thread-safe?
followups.a: A single lock around every operation, because the two stacks must move together: without that, another thread could observe the value pushed but not its minimum, and `GetMin` would be wrong. A lock-free version is much harder here than for a plain stack, since the invariant spans two structures, which is an argument for holding a single immutable node with both the value and the running minimum instead. That reduces it to one reference to swap atomically, and is how you would actually build a lock-free version.

followups.q: Why throw rather than return a sentinel when empty?
followups.a: Because there is no int value that cannot legitimately be in the stack, so any sentinel is ambiguous with real data. That is the same in-band sentinel problem as using int.MinValue for BST bounds. The alternatives are throwing, as here, matching the behaviour of .NET's own `Stack<T>.Pop`, or a `TryGetMin(out int)` pattern for callers who expect emptiness. Returning 0 or -1 silently is the one option that is actually wrong.

question: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation (postfix expression).

followups.q: Why does -7 / 2 give -3 rather than -4?
followups.a: Because C# integer division truncates toward zero rather than flooring, so -3.5 becomes -3. The RPN problem specifies exactly this behaviour, so the language happens to match. It is worth knowing that Python floors instead and would give -4, which is a genuine source of bugs when porting numeric code between the two. If the requirement were flooring, you would need an explicit adjustment when the operands have opposite signs and the division is not exact.

followups.q: How would you convert infix to postfix in the first place?
followups.a: The shunting-yard algorithm. Scan the infix tokens, output operands immediately, and push operators onto a stack, popping any operator of greater or equal precedence before pushing. Parentheses push and pop as a group. It is O(n) and produces postfix that this evaluator then consumes. Together the two are a complete expression evaluator, and that pairing is the usual follow-up once the postfix half is working.

followups.q: Suppose the expression came from user input and could be malformed or hostile.
followups.a: Then the validation matters more than the evaluation. The checks here cover too few operands, leftover operands and unknown operators, which are the three structural failures. Beyond that you would bound the input length to prevent a stack of unbounded depth, use checked arithmetic or a wider type so that overflow throws rather than wrapping silently, and return a structured error identifying the offending token rather than a generic exception. An evaluator that silently returns a wrong number on bad input is worse than one that refuses it.

question: Daily temperatures: days until a warmer temperature.

followups.q: Why is this O(n) when there is a while loop inside a for loop?
followups.a: Because each index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once across the whole run, so the total number of pop operations is bounded by n regardless of how they cluster. A single iteration might pop many entries, but that work was paid for when those entries were pushed. This amortised argument is the standard justification for every monotonic-stack algorithm, and stating it is what separates recognising the pattern from merely reproducing it.

followups.q: Why store indices rather than temperatures on the stack?
followups.a: Because the answer is a distance, which needs positions, not values. With temperatures alone you could tell that today is warmer but not how many days had passed. Storing indices also gives free access to the temperature via a lookup, so nothing is lost. It is the same reasoning as in sliding window maximum, where indices are needed to detect that an element has left the window.

followups.q: Suppose the temperatures arrived as a stream and answers were needed as soon as they were known.
followups.a: The algorithm already works that way: each day resolves some earlier days immediately, so you can emit those answers as they are determined rather than waiting for the end. The catch is that unresolved days accumulate on the stack indefinitely, so on a monotonically decreasing stream the memory grows without bound. If that mattered you would cap the wait at some horizon and flush anything older, which changes the semantics to 'warmer within k days' but bounds the memory.

question: Largest rectangle in a histogram.

followups.q: Why does the width use i - left - 1 rather than the popped index?
followups.a: Because the rectangle extends from just after the left boundary to just before the current bar, and the popped bar's own index is somewhere inside that span rather than at its edge. Once popped, the element beneath it on the stack is by construction the nearest bar strictly shorter on the left, and the current index is the nearest shorter on the right, so the span between them exclusive is the full width at that height. Using the popped index instead gives a width that is too small whenever several equal-height bars were popped in sequence.

followups.q: What is the sentinel zero for?
followups.a: It guarantees the stack empties. Without it, an increasing histogram such as [1,2,3,4,5] would leave every bar on the stack unresolved, since nothing shorter ever arrives, and the answer would be 0. Appending a virtual bar of height zero is shorter than everything, so it pops and resolves all of them. The alternative is a separate drain loop after the main loop, which duplicates the body; the sentinel keeps it to one code path.

followups.q: How does this solve the maximal rectangle in a binary matrix?
followups.a: Treat each row as the base of a histogram whose bar heights are the counts of consecutive 1s directly above, resetting to zero at a 0. Run this algorithm on each row's histogram and take the maximum, which gives O(rows x cols) overall. That is the standard solution to a problem that looks far harder than this one, and it is the reason the histogram version is worth knowing rather than being a curiosity.

followups.q: Why >= rather than > in the pop condition?
followups.a: With equal heights, popping on equality resolves the earlier bar using the later one as its right boundary, which yields a width that is too small for that particular bar. It is still correct overall, because the later equal bar is itself resolved with the full width and produces the true maximum. Using strict greater-than avoids the redundant pops and is marginally faster. Either passes, but being able to explain why the seemingly wrong one still gives the right answer is a good sign of understanding rather than memorisation.

question: Next greater element for each element in an array.

followups.q: Why does the circular version only push during the first pass?
followups.a: Because every element already has a stack entry from the first pass; pushing again would create duplicates, and each element would be assigned an answer twice, the second one potentially wrong. The second pass exists purely to let elements that found nothing in the first pass see the values that wrap around. Once an index is popped it is resolved for good, so the second pass simply drains whatever remains. Pushing twice is the usual bug and produces answers that look plausible on small inputs.

followups.q: Suppose the query were next greater element from a second array, as in the 'next greater element I' problem.
followups.a: Compute the next greater for every element of the larger array once, store the results in a dictionary keyed by value, then look up each query element. That is O(n + m) rather than the O(n x m) of searching per query. It relies on values being distinct, which that problem guarantees; with duplicates you would key by index instead and need the positions of the query elements. Precomputing into a lookup is the general move whenever the same structure is queried repeatedly.

followups.q: What other problems use this same stack?
followups.a: Largest rectangle in a histogram, where you need the nearest smaller element on each side; trapping rain water, solved in layers; the stock span problem; and removing k digits to form the smallest number, which keeps an increasing stack instead. They differ only in the comparison direction and in what is recorded on pop. Recognising that a problem is asking for 'the nearest element on one side satisfying a comparison' is the trigger for reaching for a monotonic stack.

question: Decode a string like '3[a2[c]]' → 'accaccacc'.

followups.q: Why push the prefix rather than just the count?
followups.a: Because text already built before the bracket must survive while the inner group is assembled. In "2[abc]3[cd]ef", when the second bracket opens, "abcabc" is already in the buffer and would be lost if the buffer were simply cleared. Parking it on a stack and restoring it on the closing bracket is what makes concatenation and nesting compose correctly. Forgetting it produces output containing only the last group, which is a very visible failure.

followups.q: Why accumulate the number digit by digit?
followups.a: Because counts can exceed nine, and reading a single character would turn 10 into two separate repetitions of 1 and 0. The `number * 10 + digit` idiom builds the value as the digits arrive. It is the same pattern as in the atoi problem, and the same place overflow would need considering if counts could be arbitrarily large, though here the expanded output would exhaust memory long before the counter overflowed.

followups.q: Suppose the input were adversarial, like 100000[100000[a]].
followups.a: The output would be ten billion characters and exhaust memory long before completing, so the algorithm is a denial-of-service vector if the input is untrusted. The defence is to compute the expanded length as you parse, using the nested counts, and reject the input once it exceeds a budget, rather than discovering the problem by running out of memory. This is a real class of bug, sometimes called a decompression bomb, and it also affects zip handling and XML entity expansion.

question: Basic calculator (with +, -, parentheses).

followups.q: Why does the sign need to be pushed as well as the total?
followups.a: Because a minus sign in front of a parenthesis negates the whole bracketed expression, not just its first term. In "2-(5-6)" the bracket evaluates to -1 and the saved sign of -1 turns it into +1, giving 3. Without saving the sign you would compute the bracket correctly and then add it with the wrong sign. It is the case that separates a working calculator from one that passes only the examples without a leading minus.

followups.q: How would you add multiplication and division?
followups.a: Precedence then matters, so the single running total breaks. The usual fix is to keep a stack of terms: when you meet a plus or minus, push the pending number with its sign; when you meet a times or divide, pop the last value, apply the operation immediately and push the result. Summing the stack at the end gives the answer, because higher-precedence operations have already been folded in. That is the 'basic calculator II' problem, and adding parentheses on top of it gives the full shunting-yard algorithm.

followups.q: Suppose you needed to evaluate the same expression many times with different variable values.
followups.a: Parsing on every evaluation is wasteful, so you parse once into an abstract syntax tree and then evaluate the tree repeatedly, or compile it to a delegate with expression trees in .NET, which gets you close to native speed. That is what spreadsheet engines and rules engines do. The transition from 'evaluate a string' to 'parse once, evaluate many' is the main architectural point once expressions become a hot path.

question: Implement a circular queue (ring buffer).

followups.q: Why is a count needed, and what is the alternative?
followups.a: Because with only head and tail indices, a full buffer and an empty one both have head equal to tail, so the two states are indistinguishable. The count removes the ambiguity directly. The classic alternative is to leave one slot permanently unused, so full means the tail is one behind the head; that saves a field at the cost of a slot and slightly trickier arithmetic. A third option used in lock-free ring buffers is to let the indices grow monotonically and take the modulo only when addressing, which also makes the two states distinct.

followups.q: Why derive the tail from head plus count rather than storing it?
followups.a: Because two independent indices can drift out of sync if a code path updates one and not the other, and the invariant linking them is then only implicit. Deriving the tail makes it impossible to be inconsistent, at the cost of one addition and a modulo per enqueue. It is a small example of preferring a single source of truth over redundant state, which matters far more in structures that are modified from several places.

followups.q: Where do ring buffers appear in real systems?
followups.a: Everywhere throughput matters and allocation does not. Audio and video pipelines use them to hand samples between threads without allocating, network stacks use them for packet queues, and high-performance logging uses them so the hot path never allocates. Kafka's partition log is conceptually the same idea at disk scale. The reason is always the same: fixed memory, no allocation, no shifting, and predictable cache behaviour, which together give latency you can reason about.

followups.q: How would you make this safe for one producer and one consumer on different threads?
followups.a: With a single producer and single consumer, you can avoid locks entirely: the producer only writes the tail and the consumer only writes the head, so each index has one writer. What you do need is a memory barrier, `Volatile.Write` and `Volatile.Read`, so that a write to the slot is visible before the index advance that publishes it. The derived-tail design here would need reworking, since a shared count is written by both sides and would require an interlocked update, which is exactly why real SPSC ring buffers keep separate head and tail indices.

question: Moving average from a data stream.
answer: Use a fixed-size sliding window (circular buffer or queue) and a running sum. On each new value, add it and subtract the value leaving the window (if full), then divide the sum by the current count. O(1) per query, O(window) space.

question: Valid parentheses with multiple bracket types.
answer: Stack of opening brackets; on a closing bracket, verify the top is the matching opener (pop) else invalid. A map from closing→opening simplifies checks. Empty stack at the end means valid. O(n) time, O(n) space.

question: Longest valid parentheses substring.

followups.q: What does the -1 sentinel actually do?
followups.a: It represents the position immediately before the string, so that a valid substring starting at index 0 measures correctly. With "()", the close at index 1 pops the open, leaving -1 on top, and 1 minus -1 gives 2. Without the sentinel the stack would be empty at that moment and you would need a special case to know the match began at the very start. It is the same technique as the dummy head node in linked-list problems: an artificial element that removes a boundary case.

followups.q: Why does the stack hold indices of unmatched positions rather than bracket characters?
followups.a: Because the answer is a length, so positions are what matter. The stack top after a pop is always the index just before the current valid run began, which is precisely what the length calculation needs. Storing characters would tell you whether the string is balanced but not how long the longest balanced stretch is. The `()()` case shows why: the two groups merge into one run of 4 only because the base index remains -1 throughout.

followups.q: Is there an O(1) space solution?
followups.a: Yes, a two-pass scan. Sweep left to right counting opens and closes, recording the length whenever they are equal and resetting when closes exceed opens; then sweep right to left with the roles reversed. The two passes are needed because a single left-to-right scan cannot detect a run that is invalid only due to excess opens, such as "(()", and the reverse pass catches exactly those. It is the same forwards-and-backwards trick as in the candy distribution problem.

question: Asteroid collision simulation.

followups.q: Why do -2,-1,1,2 never collide?
followups.a: Because the left-movers are already to the left of the right-movers and they are moving apart, so their paths diverge. A collision requires a right-mover positioned before a left-mover in the array, which is exactly the condition the loop guard checks: something positive on the stack and something negative arriving. Recognising that the direction pair, not the values, determines whether a collision is even possible is what makes the algorithm a single pass rather than a pairwise simulation.

followups.q: Why is the collision check a while loop rather than a single comparison?
followups.a: Because one large left-moving asteroid can destroy several smaller right-movers in succession, as in [10, 2, -5] where -5 destroys the 2 and then meets the 10 and is itself destroyed. A single comparison would leave the survivor in an inconsistent state. The loop terminates because each iteration either pops an element or sets the destroyed flag, so it cannot spin, and the amortised cost stays linear since every asteroid is popped at most once overall.

followups.q: Suppose asteroids had different speeds.
followups.a: The stack model breaks, because collisions would no longer occur strictly in array order: a fast left-mover could overtake and reach a right-mover before a nearer, slower one does. You would need to compute collision times for adjacent pairs and process them in chronological order with a priority queue, recomputing neighbours after each collision. That is a genuine discrete-event simulation, which is a considerable step up and a good way for an interviewer to probe whether you understand why the simple version works.

question: Flatten a multilevel doubly linked list.
answer: Iterate; when a node has a child, splice the child list between the node and its next (connect prev/next pointers), and continue. Use a stack to remember 'next' pointers when descending into children. O(n) time. Result is a single-level doubly linked list.

question: Partition a linked list around a value x.
answer: Build two separate lists (nodes < x and nodes >= x) using dummy heads, preserving order, then connect the first list's tail to the second's head. O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Keeps stable relative order within each partition.

question: Sort a linked list in O(n log n).

followups.q: Why merge sort rather than quicksort for a linked list?
followups.a: Because quicksort's advantages evaporate without random access. Choosing a good pivot needs indexing, partitioning in place needs bidirectional movement, and the cache locality that makes quicksort fast on arrays does not apply to scattered nodes anyway. Merge sort only walks forward and relinks, which is exactly what a singly linked list supports, and it needs no auxiliary array because merging lists is done by pointer, not by copying. That is why merging lists is O(1) extra space while merging arrays is O(n).

followups.q: Why does splitting at the second middle cause infinite recursion?
followups.a: With a two-node list, the second middle is the second node, so the split produces an empty first half and a two-node second half. The recursive call receives the same two-node list and splits it the same way forever. Starting the fast pointer at `head.Next` biases toward the first middle, guaranteeing both halves are strictly smaller. It is a one-token difference that turns a working sort into a stack overflow, and only on even-length inputs.

followups.q: How would you reach O(1) space?
followups.a: Bottom-up merge sort. Instead of recursing, merge adjacent runs of size 1, then 2, then 4, doubling each pass until the run length exceeds the list length. It needs careful bookkeeping to split and reconnect runs, but there is no call stack at all. That is what most standard library list sorts use, and it is also the structure of an external merge sort over files, where the recursion would be impossible anyway.

question: Design a max/min queue with O(1) amortized max query.
answer: Maintain a regular queue plus a monotonic deque holding candidates for the max in decreasing order. On enqueue, pop smaller values from the deque's back; on dequeue, if the front equals the deque's front, pop it. getMax returns the deque's front. Amortized O(1).

question: Simplify a Unix-style absolute path.

followups.q: Why must .. at the root be ignored rather than erroring?
followups.a: Because that is how Unix behaves: the root is its own parent, so `cd /..` leaves you at the root. Erroring would diverge from the semantics being modelled. It also matters for security: code that resolves paths and allows `..` to escape above a base directory is the classic path-traversal vulnerability, where a request for `../../etc/passwd` reaches outside the intended folder. Clamping at the root is both correct and the safe behaviour.

followups.q: Why a List rather than a Stack here?
followups.a: Because the result needs the components in original order, and `Stack<T>` enumerates newest-first, so it would have to be reversed before joining. A `List<T>` used as a stack, pushing with Add and popping from the end, gives O(1) for both operations and enumerates in the right order. It is a small reminder that the abstract data type and the concrete collection are separate choices, and the traversal order can decide the second one.

followups.q: Would you use this for real path handling?
followups.a: No. Real paths bring symbolic links, which `..` does not traverse the way lexical simplification assumes, plus case sensitivity rules, Windows drive letters and UNC prefixes, and Unicode normalisation. `Path.GetFullPath` and the platform APIs handle those, and security-sensitive code should resolve the real path and then verify it sits under the permitted root, rather than trusting lexical cleanup. The exercise is about the stack; the production answer is to use the library.

question: Maximum depth of a binary tree.

followups.q: When would the recursive version actually fail?
followups.a: On a degenerate tree, where every node has one child and the depth equals the node count. A million-node chain means a million stack frames and a StackOverflowException, which in .NET cannot be caught and kills the process outright. That is the argument for the iterative version in any code path where the tree shape is not controlled by you: parsing user-supplied JSON or XML into a tree is the classic case.

followups.q: How does minimum depth differ, and why is it trickier?
followups.a: Minimum depth is the distance to the nearest leaf, and the naive mirror of this code is wrong: taking `Math.Min` of both subtrees returns 1 for a node with only a right child, because the null left subtree reports 0. A leaf is a node with no children, so when one side is null you must take the other side's depth rather than the minimum. BFS is also the better strategy here since it can stop at the first leaf it meets instead of exploring the whole tree.

followups.q: Why snapshot queue.Count into levelSize?
followups.a: Because the loop enqueues children while iterating, so reading `queue.Count` directly inside the condition would keep consuming the next level as part of this one and the depth counter would never advance correctly. Capturing the size first fixes the boundary of the current level. That level-snapshot pattern is the backbone of every level-order problem: right-side view, level averages, zigzag traversal all use it.

question: Invert / mirror a binary tree.

followups.q: Does the traversal order matter here?
followups.a: No, and that is worth saying explicitly because it is unusual. Preorder, postorder, BFS or DFS all produce the same result, since each node's swap is independent of every other node's. Contrast it with flattening a tree to a linked list, where preorder is mandatory and any other order gives the wrong answer. Recognising which problems are order-sensitive is the more transferable point.

followups.q: What if the tree is a BST?
followups.a: Inverting a BST destroys the BST property: the in-order traversal goes from ascending to descending, so search, insert and delete all break. If the goal is to iterate in reverse order, do not invert the tree at all, just do a reversed in-order traversal, visiting right, then node, then left. That is O(h) space and leaves the structure intact, which is almost always what the caller actually wanted.

question: Check if two binary trees are identical.

followups.q: Why does the shape matter, when both trees hold the same values?
followups.a: Because a tree is defined by its structure, not just its contents. The third test case has values 1 and 2 in both trees, but one has the 2 as a left child and the other as a right child; they represent different data and behave differently under traversal. This is also why comparing two trees by their in-order traversals alone is unsound: different trees can share a traversal, which is precisely why reconstructing a tree needs two traversals rather than one.

followups.q: How would you check whether one tree is a subtree of another?
followups.a: For each node of the larger tree whose value matches the candidate root, run this identical-trees check from there. That is O(n·m) in the worst case. The faster answer is to serialise both trees to strings with explicit null markers and ask whether one is a substring of the other, which with KMP is O(n + m). The null markers are essential: without them, serialisations of different trees can collide and produce a false positive.

followups.q: Would you use this to implement Equals on a tree type?
followups.a: Only with care. Structural equality for a mutable reference type is a well-known hazard: if a tree is used as a dictionary key and then mutated, its hash changes and the entry becomes unreachable. You would also need `GetHashCode` to agree, computed over the same structure, which is O(n) on every hash. The usual guidance is to keep structural comparison as an explicit method, as here, and leave `Equals` as reference identity unless the type is immutable.

question: Check if a binary tree is symmetric.

followups.q: Why can't you just compare the left subtree to the right subtree directly?
followups.a: Because that tests identity rather than mirroring. The second test case has two identical subtrees, each with only a right child, and a direct comparison would call it symmetric; but folding the tree along its centre puts those two children on the same side, so it is not. The crosswise pairing is what encodes the reflection, and getting it wrong produces a function that passes every symmetric test case while also passing some asymmetric ones.

followups.q: Could you invert the right subtree and then compare?
followups.a: Yes, and it is a legitimate answer: mirror one side, then run the identical-trees check. It costs an extra O(n) pass and either mutates the tree or allocates a copy, so the direct crosswise comparison is better. It is worth mentioning because it shows you see the relationship between the two problems, which an interviewer often probes by asking them back to back.

followups.q: Why does the iterative version use a queue rather than a stack?
followups.a: Either works. The pairs are independent, so the order in which they are checked does not affect the result, only which mismatch is found first. A queue checks level by level, which tends to find a shallow asymmetry sooner and is easier to reason about when debugging; a stack goes depth-first and uses less memory on a wide tree. This is unlike problems such as flattening a tree, where the traversal order is load-bearing.

question: Binary tree level order traversal (BFS).

followups.q: How would you produce a zigzag traversal?
followups.a: Keep the same BFS and reverse alternate levels, either by reversing the list after building it or by inserting at the front on odd levels. Reversing afterwards is better: inserting at index 0 of a List is O(n) per insert, which makes the level O(n²), whereas a single reverse is O(n). If you want to avoid even that, build into an array and fill it from either end depending on the direction.

followups.q: Give the right-side view using this skeleton.
followups.a: Take the last node of each level, which is the element at index levelSize-1 in the inner loop. The whole change is one condition. That is the real value of the level-snapshot pattern: right-side view, level averages, maximum per level, level order bottom-up and zigzag are all the same loop with a different line inside, so learning it once covers a whole family of interview questions.

followups.q: When is BFS the wrong choice for a tree?
followups.a: When the tree is wide and shallow, because the queue holds an entire level and that can approach n, whereas DFS would use only O(h). It is also wrong whenever the problem needs information flowing up from children, such as height, diameter or subtree sums, since those are naturally postorder. BFS earns its place when the answer depends on distance from the root, which is why it is the right tool for shortest path in an unweighted graph.

question: Validate a binary search tree.

followups.q: Why long? for the bounds rather than int sentinels?
followups.a: Because using int.MinValue and int.MaxValue as 'no bound' makes a tree containing those exact values fail incorrectly: a single root node holding int.MinValue would be rejected, as the last test case shows. Widening to long gives room outside the int range, and a nullable makes the absence of a bound explicit rather than encoded as a magic value. This is the general argument against in-band sentinels, and it recurs constantly in real code.

followups.q: Should duplicates be allowed?
followups.a: The definition has to come from the interviewer, and asking is the right move. The strict version, used here, rejects equal values on both sides. Some definitions permit duplicates on the right, which changes the comparison from `>=` to `>` on one side only. Most importantly, the two conventions must not be mixed: allowing duplicates on both sides makes search ambiguous, because a value could legitimately sit in either subtree and lookups would have to explore both.

followups.q: Which of the two implementations do you prefer?
followups.a: The in-order one, for production. It is iterative so it cannot overflow the stack, it returns false as soon as the first out-of-order pair appears rather than always descending, and it only needs the previous value rather than a pair of bounds threaded through the recursion. The range version is easier to explain and the better one to reach for first in an interview, since it makes the global-versus-local insight visible, which is the thing being tested.

question: Lowest common ancestor in a BST.

followups.q: Why is a node considered its own ancestor here?
followups.a: It is a definitional choice that the standard problem makes, and it is worth confirming with the interviewer. Under it, the LCA of 2 and 4 is 2 itself, as the second test shows. The alternative definition, requiring a strict ancestor, would return 6 instead and needs extra handling once you have found the split point. Neither is more correct; what matters is stating which you are implementing, since the two produce different answers on exactly the inputs people forget to test.

followups.q: How does this change for a general binary tree with no ordering?
followups.a: You lose the ability to choose a direction, so you must search. Recurse into both subtrees looking for either target: if they are found on opposite sides the current node is the LCA, and if both come back from the same side that side's result bubbles up. That is O(n) time and O(h) space, against O(h) and O(1) here. The contrast is the point of asking both versions, because it shows exactly what the BST invariant is buying you.

followups.q: What if the values might not be in the tree at all?
followups.a: This version does not verify that, and will confidently return a node for two values that were never present. If the inputs are untrusted you need an explicit search for each first, which doubles the traversal but makes the contract honest, or a variant that tracks whether both were seen during the descent. It is the same class of issue as an algorithm that assumes a majority element exists: the guarantee lives in the problem statement, not in the code.

question: Lowest common ancestor in a binary tree (not BST).

followups.q: What happens if only one of the two values exists in the tree?
followups.a: It returns that node, as if it were the answer, which is wrong: there is no common ancestor of a present and an absent value. The usual problem statement guarantees both exist, so the code is correct under its stated contract, but shipping it without that guarantee is a bug. The fix is to carry two booleans recording whether each target was actually seen, and return null unless both were, which costs nothing asymptotically.

followups.q: How would you solve it if nodes had parent pointers?
followups.a: It becomes the same problem as finding the intersection of two linked lists. Walk up from each node collecting ancestors, and the first shared one is the answer; with a set of one node's ancestors that is O(h) time and O(h) space. Better still, compute both depths, advance the deeper pointer to match, then step both up together for O(1) space. That equivalence between tree ancestry and list intersection is a satisfying thing to point out.

followups.q: What if you must answer many LCA queries on the same tree?
followups.a: Then O(n) per query is wasteful and you preprocess instead. Binary lifting stores each node's 2^k-th ancestor, giving O(n log n) build and O(log n) per query. The Euler-tour plus sparse-table approach reduces LCA to a range-minimum query and answers in O(1) after O(n log n) preprocessing. Recognising that repeated queries change the right answer entirely is the real content of the follow-up.

question: Binary tree in-order/pre-order/post-order traversal (iterative).

followups.q: Why push right before left in the pre-order version?
followups.a: Because a stack reverses the order of insertion. Pre-order must visit left before right, so left has to come off the stack first, which means it must go on last. Pushing left first would produce root, right, left, which is the mirror image. It is a small thing that is easy to get backwards, and the reliable way to reason about it is to trace a three-node tree rather than trying to remember the rule.

followups.q: Is the reverse trick for post-order cheating?
followups.a: It is a legitimate and widely used solution, but an interviewer may ask for the version without the final reverse, since that one needs O(n) extra ordering work and cannot stream results. The honest single-stack post-order tracks the last visited node and only pops a node once its right child has been processed, or uses a second stack. Say which you are giving and why, because offering the reverse trick while showing you know its limitation reads much better than presenting it as the only way.

followups.q: Can you traverse with O(1) space?
followups.a: Yes, with Morris traversal. It temporarily rewires the tree, making each node's in-order predecessor point to it as a thread, follows the thread back up, and then restores the original pointer. That gives O(n) time and O(1) space with no stack at all. The catch is that it mutates the tree during traversal, so it is unusable if anything else can read the tree concurrently, which is worth stating alongside the trick.

question: Construct a binary tree from preorder and inorder traversals.

followups.q: Why must the left subtree be built before the right?
followups.a: Because the preorder pointer is shared and advances as nodes are consumed. Preorder is root, then the entire left subtree, then the entire right subtree, so the values immediately after the root belong to the left. Building the right first would hand it the left subtree's values. The ordering is not a style choice, it is load-bearing, and it is why the shared `_pre` index works at all without passing explicit ranges for the preorder array.

followups.q: Could you build the tree from inorder and postorder instead? What about preorder and postorder?
followups.a: Inorder plus postorder works the same way: postorder gives the root at the *end*, so you consume it backwards and build the right subtree before the left. Preorder plus postorder does not work in general, because without inorder you cannot tell which side a subtree sits on. A node with a single child produces the same preorder and postorder whether that child is on the left or the right, so the tree is ambiguous. It is only unique if the tree is guaranteed full, with every node having zero or two children.

followups.q: Suppose the tree contains duplicate values. What breaks?
followups.a: The value-to-index map, because a value no longer identifies a unique position in inorder; the later duplicate silently overwrites the earlier entry and the split happens in the wrong place. Worse, the problem itself becomes ambiguous: with duplicates the two traversals may not determine a unique tree at all. The realistic fix is to work with node identities or positions rather than values, which usually means the traversals must carry index information, and it is worth saying that the standard problem statement quietly guarantees uniqueness for exactly this reason.

followups.q: The static fields make this non-reentrant. Would you ship that?
