followups.a: No. Two threads calling `BuildTree` at once would trample each other's `_pre` and map, producing corrupted trees with no exception. In an interview it keeps the code short and is worth flagging out loud; in production I would pass the state explicitly or wrap the recursion in a small private class holding the map and the index as instance fields. It is the same argument as passing `best` by ref in the diameter problem rather than using a field.

question: Right side view of a binary tree.

followups.q: Why isn't the answer simply the rightmost path from the root?
followups.a: Because visibility depends on depth, not on which child you are. The second test case has a node 4 hanging off the left subtree at a depth the right subtree never reaches, so it is visible from the right even though every step to it went left. The last case makes the point sharply: a purely left-leaning tree is entirely visible from the right. Walking the right children only would return 1,3 and 1 respectively, both wrong.

followups.q: Can you do it depth-first?
followups.a: Yes, and it is neat: traverse right subtree before left, carrying the current depth, and record a node only when the depth first exceeds the number of values collected so far. Because the right side is visited first at every level, the first node seen at each new depth is the visible one. It uses O(h) space instead of O(w), which is a real win on a wide tree, and it is a good answer to give after the BFS version.

followups.q: How would you get the left side view, or the top view?
followups.a: The left side view is the same code taking index 0 of each level instead of the last. The top view is different in kind: it needs a horizontal offset per node, decrementing going left and incrementing going right, recording the first node seen at each offset, which requires BFS specifically since DFS could reach a deeper node at an offset first. That distinction, where BFS is mandatory rather than merely convenient, is worth making explicit.

question: Path sum: does a root-to-leaf path sum to a target?

followups.q: Why does an empty tree return false even when the target is 0?
followups.a: Because the question asks whether a root-to-leaf path exists with that sum, and an empty tree has no paths at all, so no path can satisfy anything. Returning true for a target of 0 would be treating the absence of a path as a path of sum zero, which also breaks the recursion: a node with one null child would then accept a path descending into nothing. The fourth test case pins this down.

followups.q: Can you stop early once the running sum exceeds the target?
followups.a: Only if every value is guaranteed non-negative, in which case the sum grows monotonically and overshooting means the branch is dead. With negative values allowed, as in the last test case, a path can exceed the target and come back, so pruning would produce wrong answers. This is the same monotonicity question that decides whether a sliding window is valid for subarray sums, and the honest answer is to ask about the value range before optimising.

followups.q: How does path sum III differ?
followups.a: It counts paths that may start and end anywhere, as long as they go downward, so the root-to-leaf structure disappears. The efficient solution uses prefix sums along the current root-to-node path with a hash map of counts, exactly as in subarray sum equals k, giving O(n). The crucial extra step is removing the current node's prefix from the map as the recursion unwinds, otherwise sums leak across sibling branches. It is a nice demonstration that a tree path problem can reduce to an array technique.

question: Binary tree maximum path sum (any node to any node).

followups.q: Why does the method return one side but record both?
followups.a: Because a path is a simple path: it cannot branch. A path that uses both of a node's children already turns at that node, so it cannot then continue upward through the parent without revisiting the node. The parent therefore needs the best straight-line descent, which is the node plus the better single side. Recording both while returning one is how a single traversal answers a question about paths that turn anywhere. Returning the recorded value instead is the standard bug, and it yields sums for paths that are not paths.

followups.q: Why initialise best to int.MinValue rather than 0?
followups.a: Because the path must contain at least one node, so an all-negative tree has a negative answer, and starting at 0 would wrongly return 0 for it. The last two test cases pin this down: a single -3 node must give -3. Note the asymmetry with the clamp inside the function, which is correct precisely because skipping a subtree is allowed while skipping every node is not.

followups.q: How is this related to Kadane's algorithm?
followups.a: It is Kadane's on a tree. Kadane's asks whether to extend the previous run or start fresh, which is exactly what `Math.Max(0, gain)` decides for each branch, and it tracks a global best separately from the running value, just as here. Seeing maximum subarray, maximum path sum and house robber III as the same recurrence over different structures is the point of the cluster, and saying so out loud lands well.

question: Count the number of nodes in a complete binary tree efficiently.
answer: Use the complete-tree property: compute left height (leftmost path) and right height (rightmost path). If equal, the subtree is perfect with 2^h - 1 nodes; else recurse on both children. O(log^2 n) time instead of O(n).

question: Kth smallest element in a BST.

followups.q: What if the tree is modified frequently and this query is hot?
followups.a: Augment each node with the size of its subtree. Then finding the kth smallest is a descent: compare k against the left subtree's size to decide whether to go left, take the current node, or go right with k reduced. That is O(h) rather than O(h + k), and insertions and deletions maintain the counts in O(h) as they already walk the path. This is the standard order-statistic tree, and proposing it is the expected answer to this follow-up.

followups.q: Why iterative rather than recursive here?
followups.a: Because the early exit is awkward to express in a recursive in-order traversal: you have to thread a counter and a found flag through every frame, or throw an exception to unwind, both of which are uglier than the explicit stack. The iterative version also cannot overflow the stack on a degenerate tree, which a recursive version can. When a traversal needs to stop partway, an explicit stack is usually the cleaner tool.

followups.q: How would you get the kth LARGEST instead?
followups.a: Mirror the traversal: go right, visit, then left, which yields descending order, and take the kth. It is a two-character change and avoids the temptation to compute the total node count and ask for the (n-k+1)th smallest, which requires an extra full traversal to count. That reversed in-order walk is the same technique that answers 'convert a BST to a greater tree', where each node is replaced by the sum of all larger values.

question: Serialize and deserialize a binary tree.

followups.q: Why are the null markers essential?
followups.a: Because without them the encoding is ambiguous: the pre-order sequence 1,2 could mean 2 is the left child of 1 or the right child, and those are different trees. That ambiguity is the same reason reconstructing a tree from a single traversal is impossible, and why the classic problem gives you both pre-order and in-order. The null markers restore the missing information by making the shape explicit, which is why they cost space but buy a single-traversal encoding.

followups.q: This uses a delimiter and int.Parse. What breaks in production?
followups.a: Several things. If node values were strings rather than ints, any value containing a comma or a '#' would corrupt the format, so you would need escaping or a length-prefixed encoding. Malformed input causes int.Parse to throw rather than reporting a parse failure, so a real deserialiser should validate and return a clear error. And a deeply skewed tree overflows the stack in both directions. A production version would use a length-prefixed binary format and an explicit stack, which is roughly what protobuf does.

followups.q: How would you serialise an n-ary tree, where nodes have any number of children?
followups.a: Write each node followed by its child count, then its children recursively. The count replaces the null markers, since it says exactly how many sub-trees to consume, and it generalises to any arity without a fixed left and right. The alternative is a sentinel marking the end of a child list, which is closer to the format here. Either works; the count version is more compact and the sentinel version is easier to read by eye.

question: Diameter of a binary tree.

followups.q: Why must the recursion return height rather than diameter?
followups.a: Because the two quantities compose differently. A node's height is one plus the larger child height, which is a local rule. Its diameter is not derivable from its children's diameters, since the longest path through it depends on how deep each side reaches, not on how long the paths within each side were. So the traversal computes the composable quantity and accumulates the non-composable one in a side variable. That pattern, return one thing and accumulate another, recurs in maximum path sum and house robber III.

followups.q: Edges or nodes: which is the diameter?
followups.a: Ask, because both conventions exist and they differ by one. This implementation counts edges, so a single node has diameter 0 and the last test case gives 4. If the problem counts nodes on the path, the answer is edges plus one, and a single node has diameter 1. Getting this wrong is an off-by-one that passes most tests and fails the degenerate ones, which is exactly why the empty and single-node cases are in the output above.

followups.q: Why pass best by ref rather than using a field?
followups.a: To keep the method free of shared mutable state, which makes it safe to call concurrently on different trees and obvious to read. A private field would work in single-threaded code but turns the method into something that cannot be reentered, and two threads calling it at once would corrupt each other's results. The alternative is returning a tuple of height and best diameter, which is purely functional and arguably cleaner, at the cost of slightly noisier code.

question: Check if a binary tree is height-balanced.

followups.q: Why is the naive version O(n squared)?
followups.a: Because it asks each node for the heights of its subtrees, and computing a height is itself a full traversal of that subtree. So a node at depth d has its subtree walked once for every ancestor above it. On a degenerate tree that is the classic 1+2+3+...+n sum, giving quadratic time. The fix is the standard one for this shape of problem: compute the expensive quantity once on the way back up and pass it to the parent, rather than asking for it again on the way down.

followups.q: Is a sentinel of -1 safe here?
followups.a: Yes, because a real height is always at least 0, so -1 is outside the valid range and cannot be confused with data. That is the test any in-band sentinel must pass, and it is why int.MinValue fails as a BST bound while -1 succeeds here. If you disliked it, the alternatives are returning a tuple of height and a balanced flag, or a nullable int, both of which are more explicit at a small cost in noise.

followups.q: What definition of balanced do real self-balancing trees use?
followups.a: AVL trees use exactly this one, a height difference of at most one at every node, which keeps them tightly balanced but makes insertions rotate more often. Red-black trees use a looser colour-based invariant that allows one path to be up to twice as long as another, trading slightly worse lookup depth for noticeably cheaper insertion and deletion. That is why .NET's SortedDictionary and most standard libraries use red-black rather than AVL: mutation cost usually matters more than the last few percent of lookup depth.

question: Flatten a binary tree to a linked list (preorder, in-place).

followups.q: Why does the traversal order matter here when it did not for inverting a tree?
followups.a: Because the output is a sequence, not a set of independent per-node edits. Inverting swaps each node's children, and those swaps commute, so any order works. Flattening must produce nodes in a specific linear order, and only preorder gives root before left before right. Attempting it with postorder or level order yields a chain in the wrong sequence. Knowing which problems are order-sensitive is the transferable lesson, and this pair makes the contrast cleanly.

followups.q: Suppose you are asked for the simplest correct version, not the cleverest. What would you write?
followups.a: A reversed-preorder recursion: visit right, then left, then node, keeping a reference to the previously visited node, and at each node set `right = previous` and `left = null`. It is six lines and obviously correct, at the cost of O(h) stack space. I would offer that first, then the O(1) Morris-style version above as the improvement. Leading with the clever one risks spending the interview debugging pointer surgery when the interviewer only wanted to see that you understood preorder.

followups.q: Suppose another thread is reading this tree while Flatten runs. What happens?
followups.a: It sees a corrupt structure. Mid-flatten the tree is neither the original nor the result: subtrees have been relocated and some nodes are temporarily reachable by two paths. A concurrent reader could traverse into a partially rewired region and, in the worst case, loop. There is no cheap fix because the operation mutates in place by design; you either take an exclusive lock, flatten a copy, or build an immutable result. That is the general cost of in-place algorithms, and the reason `List<T>` throws if the collection is modified during enumeration.

question: Populate next right pointers in each node (perfect binary tree).
answer: Use established next pointers to traverse each level and link the next level: for each node, connect left.next = right, and right.next = node.next.left (if node.next exists). Move down leftmost each level. O(n) time, O(1) space (using the tree's own pointers).

question: Convert a sorted array to a height-balanced BST.

followups.q: Is the answer unique?
followups.a: No. With an even number of elements there are two middle choices, and either gives a valid height-balanced BST, so a test asserting one exact tree is over-specified. `low + (high - low) / 2` picks the left middle, which is why [1,3] produces 1 as the root with 3 on the right; picking the right middle would produce 3 with 1 on the left. Both are correct. Interview graders usually accept any valid answer, and it is worth saying which convention you chose rather than leaving it implicit.

followups.q: Suppose the input is a sorted linked list instead of an array. What changes?
followups.a: You lose O(1) access to the middle, so naively finding it each time costs O(n) per level and the whole build becomes O(n log n). Two better options: walk the list once into an array and use this algorithm for O(n) time and O(n) space, or build bottom-up in O(n) time and O(log n) space by recursing on the *count* of elements and consuming the list in order as the recursion unwinds, which produces the nodes in inorder sequence. The second is the elegant answer and the one an interviewer is fishing for.

followups.q: Why does this guarantee balance, when a normal BST insertion loop would not?
followups.a: Because inserting sorted values one at a time always appends to the same side, producing a degenerate chain of height n, which is the classic worst case and the reason self-balancing trees exist. Building from the middle outwards never makes that choice: each recursion splits the remaining range into two halves differing by at most one element, so the height difference at every node is bounded by one automatically. No rotations are needed because the structure is chosen rather than repaired.

question: Number of islands (connected components in a grid).

followups.q: Why mark cells on enqueue rather than on dequeue?
followups.a: Because a cell can be reached from several neighbours. If you only mark it when it comes off the queue, it can be enqueued multiple times before the first one is processed, which in the worst case makes the queue grow far beyond the grid size and the algorithm do redundant work. Marking at enqueue time guarantees every cell enters the queue exactly once. It is a small change that turns a subtly quadratic implementation into a linear one.

followups.q: The grid is a million by a million and cannot fit in memory. Now what?
followups.a: Process it in tiles that do fit, running the count within each tile, then reconcile islands that straddle tile boundaries by recording the border cells and unioning components across edges with a disjoint-set structure. That is the standard connected-components-at-scale approach and maps cleanly onto a distributed job. The insight to state is that only the boundaries need to cross tile lines, so the merge data is proportional to the perimeter rather than the area.

followups.q: How would you solve it with union-find instead?
followups.a: Give every land cell an id, union it with its right and down neighbours if they are also land, then count the distinct roots. With path compression and union by rank it is effectively O(rows × cols). It is more code than BFS for this problem, so it is not the first answer, but it becomes the right one when islands must be counted repeatedly as cells are added, since union-find handles incremental connection while BFS would need a full rescan each time.

question: Clone a graph.

followups.q: What exactly goes wrong if you register the clone after recursing instead of before?
followups.a: Infinite recursion on any cycle. Cloning node 1 would recurse into 2, which recurses back into 1, which is not yet in the map, so it clones 1 again and the process never terminates, ending in a stack overflow. Registering first means the second visit finds the partially built clone and returns it, and the neighbour list is filled in as the outer call completes. It is the same fix-up-later technique that object serialisers and dependency injection containers use to handle circular references.

followups.q: Suppose the graph is disconnected. Does this still work?
followups.a: Not from a single start node: traversal only reaches the component containing it, so other components are silently missing. The problem statement usually promises connectivity. If it did not, you would need the full node list and a loop that starts a fresh traversal from every unvisited node, accumulating into the same map so shared structure is preserved. That distinction between 'clone reachable from here' and 'clone the whole graph' is worth clarifying before writing anything.

followups.q: Would you use recursion here in production?
followups.a: Probably not. Depth is bounded by the number of nodes, so a long chain of ten thousand nodes risks a stack overflow, which in .NET cannot be caught. The iterative version is the same algorithm with an explicit stack or queue: create the clone on first sight, push the original, and wire neighbours when it is processed. Slightly more code, no depth limit. Recursion is fine for balanced trees where depth is logarithmic, and risky for graphs and lists where it is not.

question: Course schedule: can you finish all courses (cycle detection in a directed graph)?

followups.q: How does the DFS version detect a cycle, and why are three colours needed?
followups.a: DFS marks nodes white for unvisited, grey for on the current recursion stack, and black for fully explored. Meeting a grey node means an edge back into the path you are currently on, which is a cycle. Two states are not enough: meeting an already-visited black node is perfectly normal in a DAG, since two branches can converge on the same node, so treating any revisit as a cycle gives false positives. The grey state is precisely what distinguishes a back edge from a cross edge.

followups.q: Suppose some prerequisites are optional, or courses run in fixed semesters. How does the model change?
followups.a: Optional prerequisites mean the graph is no longer a hard constraint set, so you would model them as soft edges and optimise rather than merely validate, which turns it into a scheduling problem rather than a topological sort. Fixed semesters add a capacity constraint: each round you can take at most k courses, so instead of dequeuing one at a time you process whole levels, and the answer becomes the number of rounds. That levelled variant is the 'minimum semesters to finish' problem and falls straight out of the same indegree machinery.

followups.q: Why Kahn's rather than DFS here?
followups.a: Both are O(V + E) and both are correct. Kahn's is iterative, so there is no stack-depth risk on a deep dependency chain, it produces the ordering directly rather than as a reversed postorder, and its failure mode is easy to report: the remaining nodes with non-zero indegree are exactly the ones involved in cycles, which is genuinely useful in a build tool or package manager. DFS is more compact and better when you also want the specific cycle path for an error message.

question: Course schedule II: return a valid course order.

followups.q: The second case could also be 0,2,1,3. Is the answer unique?
followups.a: No, and that matters for testing. Any ordering respecting the dependencies is valid, and courses 1 and 2 are independent so either may come first. A unit test asserting one exact array is fragile: it would break if the queue were swapped for a stack, or if the adjacency lists were built in a different order. The right assertion is a property check, that every prerequisite appears before its dependent, which is also a useful two-line helper to offer in the interview.

followups.q: Suppose the interviewer wants the lexicographically smallest valid order.
followups.a: Swap the queue for a min-heap. Instead of taking any ready course, always take the smallest-numbered one available. That makes it O((V + E) log V) rather than linear, but guarantees a deterministic, lexicographically minimal ordering. This is exactly what package managers and build systems do when they want reproducible output, since a non-deterministic build order makes caching and debugging much harder.

followups.q: Where does this appear in real systems?
followups.a: Everywhere dependencies are resolved. NuGet and npm order package installation this way, MSBuild orders project compilation, database migration tools order schema changes, and Excel uses it to decide the order in which to recalculate cells. The cycle case is what produces the familiar 'circular dependency detected' error, and the fact that the algorithm can also name the offending nodes is why those error messages can list the specific cycle rather than just complaining.

question: Rotting oranges (multi-source BFS).

followups.q: Why does the fresh == 0 early return matter?
followups.a: Because a grid with no fresh oranges takes zero minutes, but without the check the loop would exit immediately with `minutes` at 0 anyway, so it looks redundant. It stops being redundant in the variant where you continue counting while the queue drains: then the final level, in which nothing new rots, would still increment the counter and return one minute too many. Guarding both on the queue and on the remaining fresh count is what keeps the level count honest, which is the usual off-by-one in this problem.

followups.q: Suppose rotting spreads diagonally too, or at different speeds per direction.
followups.a: Diagonal spread is a one-line change to eight direction offsets, and the algorithm is unchanged because every edge still has equal weight. Different speeds per direction breaks BFS entirely: the grid becomes a weighted graph, and the shortest time is no longer the fewest steps. You would switch to Dijkstra with a priority queue keyed on elapsed time. That is the cleanest illustration of when BFS stops being valid, and it is a common way for an interviewer to escalate this question.

followups.q: Why is multi-source BFS correct, rather than just convenient?
followups.a: Because BFS explores in order of distance from the frontier, and seeding the queue with all sources makes the initial frontier the set of all sources at distance zero. The first time any cell is reached, it is reached by the shortest path from the nearest source, which is exactly the semantics of simultaneous spread. Running separate searches and taking the minimum would give the same answer at k times the cost, so the multi-source version is not an approximation, it is the same result computed once.

question: Word ladder: shortest transformation sequence length.

followups.q: Why generate neighbours instead of precomputing the adjacency list?
followups.a: Because comparing every pair of words is quadratic in the dictionary size, which is ruinous for a realistic word list of tens of thousands of entries. Generating candidates costs 26 times the word length per word, which is a small constant and independent of the dictionary size. The trade-off flips only for very long words over a large alphabet, where a wildcard-bucket preprocessing step, grouping words by patterns like `h*t`, becomes the better option.

followups.q: Suppose the dictionary is huge and the path is long. What would you do differently?
followups.a: Bidirectional BFS. Search forward from the start and backward from the end simultaneously, always expanding the smaller frontier, and stop when they meet. Because the frontier grows exponentially with depth, meeting in the middle roughly square-roots the number of nodes explored: two searches of depth d/2 instead of one of depth d. It is the standard optimisation for this problem and typically the difference between passing and timing out on the large test cases.

followups.q: Why remove words from the set rather than keeping a separate visited collection?
followups.a: It is the same thing with less bookkeeping: a word that has been enqueued must never be enqueued again, and removing it from the candidate set enforces that in the same operation that tests membership. `HashSet.Remove` returns whether the item was present, so one call both checks and marks. The one caveat is that it destroys the caller's collection if you do not copy it first, which is why the code builds its own HashSet from the input list rather than mutating what was passed in.

question: Pacific Atlantic water flow.

followups.q: Why is the comparison >= rather than > when walking uphill?
followups.a: Because water flows to a cell of equal or lower height, so reversing that means you may step to a neighbour of equal or greater height. Using a strict greater-than would break on plateaus: a flat region touching the ocean would be marked unreachable beyond its first cell, which the third test case would expose immediately. Equal heights are exactly the case people forget, and flat terrain is common in real input.

followups.q: Why is starting from the oceans better than starting from each cell?
followups.a: Starting from each cell means up to rows times cols separate searches, each potentially visiting the whole grid, so O((rc)^2) in the worst case. Starting from the borders runs two traversals total, each visiting every cell at most once, for O(rc). It is the same complement trick as the surrounded-regions problem: the question 'which cells can reach the ocean' is expensive per cell but cheap when asked once from the destination, because reachability is transitive and can be shared.

followups.q: Suppose diagonal flow were allowed, or there were three oceans.
followups.a: Diagonal flow is a one-line change to eight offsets, since nothing in the reasoning depends on the number of directions. Three oceans generalise just as cleanly: keep one reachability grid per ocean and intersect all of them, which is why the code uses separate boolean grids rather than a single two-bit mask. The structure of the solution, one reverse traversal per destination followed by an intersection, is what makes it extend without redesign.

question: Surrounded regions: capture 'O's not connected to the border.

followups.q: Why work from the border inward rather than testing each region for enclosure?
followups.a: Because testing a region for enclosure means exploring it fully and checking whether any cell touches an edge, which is the same work but with far more bookkeeping: you must collect each region's cells, decide the verdict, then go back and flip them. Starting from the border makes the property a simple reachability question with a single answer per cell and no grouping at all. It is a good example of solving the complement because the complement has a simpler definition.

followups.q: Suppose the board is enormous and mutating the input is not allowed.
followups.a: Then the 'S' marker is unavailable and you need a separate visited structure, typically a bit array of the same dimensions, which is one bit per cell rather than a full copy. The algorithm is otherwise unchanged. It is worth noting that the marker trick is really a way of borrowing the input as scratch space, which is fine for an interview and often unacceptable in production, since callers rarely expect a method named Solve to leave intermediate state behind if it throws part way through.

followups.q: How would union-find solve this instead?
followups.a: Create a virtual node representing the outside, union every border 'O' with it, and union each 'O' with its 'O' neighbours. At the end, any 'O' not connected to the virtual node is enclosed and gets flipped. It is a neat formulation and the standard way to handle the incremental version of this problem, where cells are added over time and re-running a flood fill each step would be wasteful. For a single static board, flood fill is simpler and faster.

question: Dijkstra's shortest path in a weighted graph.

followups.q: Why exactly does Dijkstra fail with negative weights?
followups.a: Because the greedy argument collapses. Settling a node assumes no shorter route can appear later, which holds only if every additional edge adds non-negative cost. With a negative edge, a longer-looking path can become cheaper after traversing it, so a node settled early may need revising, and the algorithm never revisits it. Bellman-Ford handles negatives by relaxing every edge V-1 times, at O(VE), and a further pass detects negative cycles, for which no shortest path exists at all.

followups.q: Why check settled[node] instead of decreasing the key in the heap?
followups.a: Because .NET's PriorityQueue has no decrease-key operation, and neither do most standard library heaps. The lazy approach pushes a duplicate entry at the better distance and skips stale pops, which is simpler and performs well in practice at the cost of a heap that can hold up to E entries rather than V. A Fibonacci heap gives the textbook O(E + V log V) with real decrease-key, but its constants are poor enough that the lazy binary-heap version is usually faster on real graphs.

followups.q: Suppose you need the actual route, not just the distance.
followups.a: Keep a parent array, recording which node produced each improvement during relaxation, then walk backwards from the destination and reverse. It is the same parent-pointer technique that recovers the coin list in coin change or the alignment in edit distance: the algorithm computes the cost, a parallel array remembers the decision, and a backward walk reconstructs it. Cost is one extra array and O(path length) to rebuild.

followups.q: Suppose this is a road network and you need it to be much faster.
followups.a: Add a heuristic and it becomes A*: prioritise by distance so far plus an estimate of the distance remaining, such as straight-line distance, which steers the search toward the goal instead of expanding uniformly in all directions. A* is optimal as long as the heuristic never overestimates. Beyond that, real routing engines precompute contraction hierarchies or landmark distances, which turn continent-scale queries into milliseconds by doing most of the work offline.

question: Network delay time / single-source shortest path with weights.
answer: Dijkstra from the source with a min-heap; the answer is the maximum finalized distance (time for the signal to reach all nodes), or -1 if some node is unreachable. O((V+E) log V) time. Bellman-Ford (O(VE)) handles negative weights.

question: Detect a cycle in an undirected graph (Union-Find).

followups.q: How does the DFS version differ, and what is its trap?
followups.a: DFS detects a cycle by finding an edge to an already-visited node that is not the parent you arrived from. The parent check is the trap: without it, every single edge looks like a cycle, because from node b you can always see a. Passing the parent down is the fix, and note it must exclude only the specific edge used, not every occurrence of that node, which is why a parallel edge between the same pair genuinely is a cycle and must still be reported.

followups.q: Why does union-find not need a parent check?
followups.a: Because it never traverses. It asks a set-membership question, whether these two nodes are already connected by some earlier edge, and the edge currently being processed has not yet been added to any set. So there is no way for the edge to see itself. That immunity to the parent problem is a good reason to prefer union-find for undirected cycle detection, quite apart from the incremental advantage.

followups.q: Suppose the graph is directed. Does this approach still work?
followups.a: No. Union-find has no notion of direction, so it would report the two edges a to b and a to c joined by b to c as a cycle when directionally there is none. Directed cycle detection needs either DFS with the three-colour scheme, where a grey node on the current stack signals a back edge, or Kahn's algorithm, where leftover nodes with non-zero indegree sit on cycles. Applying an undirected technique to a directed graph is one of the more common conceptual errors in this area.

question: Number of connected components in an undirected graph.

followups.q: When would you choose union-find over traversal?
followups.a: When edges arrive over time and the count must stay current. Traversal answers a static question and would have to re-run from scratch after each new edge, whereas union-find absorbs an edge in near-constant amortised time. It is also the natural fit when there is no explicit node list to iterate, or when the graph is too large to build adjacency lists for. Traversal wins when you need more than connectivity, such as the actual members of each component or distances within it.

followups.q: What do path compression and union by rank actually buy you?
followups.a: Without them, a sequence of unions can build a linked-list-shaped tree and each Find degrades to O(n). Union by rank keeps the shallower tree under the deeper one so depth grows logarithmically at worst, and path compression flattens the path on every lookup. Together they give an amortised cost of the inverse Ackermann function, which is below 5 for any input that fits in the universe, so effectively constant. Using only one of the two is still good; using neither is a real performance bug.

followups.q: Suppose the graph is directed. Does this still count components?
followups.a: No, and this is a common trap. These algorithms treat edges as bidirectional, so they compute weakly connected components: groups that would be connected if you ignored direction. Strongly connected components, where every node can reach every other following the arrows, need Tarjan's or Kosaraju's algorithm. The distinction matters in practice, for instance in dependency graphs, where a strongly connected component is precisely a circular dependency.

question: Is a graph a valid tree?

followups.q: Why is checking the edge count plus acyclicity enough? Don't you also need connectivity?
followups.a: They imply each other given the count. With exactly n-1 edges, suppose the graph were disconnected: each component with k nodes and no cycle has k-1 edges, so c components would have n-c edges total, which is fewer than n-1 whenever c exceeds 1. So n-1 edges plus acyclic forces a single component. The last test case shows why the count alone is not enough: three nodes with two edges both between the same pair passes the count but forms a cycle and leaves a node isolated.

followups.q: Suppose the input might contain self-loops or duplicate edges. Does this hold up?
followups.a: Yes, and the sixth test case demonstrates it: a duplicated edge is caught because the second copy finds both endpoints already in the same set. A self-loop is caught the same way, since Find of a node equals itself. This is a nice property of the union-find formulation; a naive 'count edges and check connectivity' approach without cycle detection would wrongly accept both. Always ask whether the input is a simple graph, because the answer changes which checks are sufficient.

followups.q: How would you do this with BFS or DFS instead?
followups.a: Traverse from node 0, counting the nodes reached and watching for an edge to a visited node that is not the one you came from. The graph is a tree if the traversal reaches all n nodes and finds no such edge. Same O(V + E), and it has the advantage of not needing the edge-count shortcut. The parent-tracking detail is the same trap as in undirected cycle detection, which is the main reason the union-find version is less error-prone to write under pressure.

question: Minimum spanning tree (Kruskal's or Prim's).
answer: Kruskal's: sort edges by weight, add each edge if it connects two different components (Union-Find), until n-1 edges. Prim's: grow the MST from a start node using a min-heap of crossing edges. Both O(E log E) / O(E log V). MST connects all nodes with minimum total edge weight.

question: Check if a graph is bipartite.

followups.q: What is the precise characterisation of a bipartite graph?
followups.a: A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd-length cycle. That is why a triangle fails and a square passes: colouring alternates along a cycle, so returning to the start with the correct colour requires an even number of steps. It also means a tree or a forest is always bipartite, having no cycles at all, and that checking bipartiteness is really odd-cycle detection wearing a different name.

followups.q: Why must the outer loop start a traversal from every node?
followups.a: Because the graph may be disconnected, and a single traversal only colours one component. The fourth test case is built for exactly this: the first component is a simple edge and perfectly bipartite, and stopping there would return true while a triangle lurks in the second component. Forgetting the outer loop is the most common bug here, and it passes any test data that happens to be connected, which is most casual test data.

followups.q: Suppose you need to know which side each node belongs to, not just whether it is possible.
followups.a: The colour array already holds it: the nodes coloured 1 form one side and those coloured -1 the other. That is the point of using a two-valued colour rather than a boolean visited flag, and it costs nothing extra. It matters because most real uses of bipartiteness need the partition, for instance to run a maximum bipartite matching for job assignment, or to lay out a graph with the two groups on opposite sides of a diagram.

followups.q: Would DFS work equally well?
followups.a: Yes, with the same colouring rule, and it is a smaller amount of code. The practical difference is that a recursive DFS can overflow the stack on a long path, and that BFS tends to find a conflict closer to the start node, which makes for a better error message if you are reporting why the graph failed. Neither is more correct, since the property does not depend on traversal order, unlike problems such as topological sort where it does.

question: Implement a Trie (prefix tree) with insert, search, startsWith.

followups.q: Dictionary per node or a fixed array of 26?
followups.a: An `int[26]`-style array of child references is faster and avoids hashing, but every node pays for 26 slots whether or not it uses them, which is wasteful for sparse tries and impossible for a large alphabet. A dictionary costs more per lookup but only stores real children, and works for any character set including Unicode. The rule of thumb is arrays for small fixed alphabets with dense branching near the root, dictionaries otherwise. Production tries often use both, arrays near the root and dictionaries deeper where branching thins out.

followups.q: Why use a trie rather than a HashSet, which also gives O(1) lookup?
followups.a: For exact-match lookup a hash set is better: simpler and usually faster. The trie earns its place the moment you need prefix queries, because a hash set cannot answer 'every word starting with app' without scanning everything. Autocomplete, IP routing tables, and word-search-on-a-grid all need exactly that. If the only operations were Insert and Search, using a trie would be over-engineering, and saying so shows judgement rather than just knowledge.

followups.q: Suppose you must also delete words. How does that work?
followups.a: Walk to the end of the word and clear its IsWord flag, which is the easy half. The subtle half is pruning: a node may now be useless, but only if it has no children and is not itself the end of another word. So you unwind back up the path deleting nodes while both conditions hold, and stop at the first node that fails either. Deleting 'app' from a trie also containing 'apple' must prune nothing at all, which is the test case that catches a naive implementation.

followups.q: Suppose the trie holds ten million words and memory is the constraint. What would you change?
followups.a: The per-node dictionary overhead dominates at that scale, so the usual moves are a radix tree, which compresses chains of single-child nodes into one edge holding a whole substring, or a double-array trie or DAWG, which merges identical suffixes so shared word endings are stored once. A DAWG can cut memory dramatically for natural-language dictionaries. The trade-off is that these structures are far harder to update, so they suit a build-once-query-many workload such as a shipped spell checker.

question: Word search II (find multiple words in a grid using a Trie).
answer: Build a Trie of the words, then DFS from each cell following Trie edges, marking visited cells; when a Trie node marks a word end, record it. Prune Trie branches once matched to speed up. O(cells * 4^L) worst case, much faster with Trie pruning.

question: Alien dictionary: derive character order from sorted words.
answer: Build a graph from adjacent word pairs: the first differing character gives an ordering edge. Topologically sort the characters (Kahn's). Detect invalid input (a longer word before its prefix) and cycles. The topological order is the alien alphabet. O(total characters) time.

question: Climbing stairs: how many ways to reach step n taking 1 or 2 steps.

followups.q: Why return long rather than int?
followups.a: Because the answer is Fibonacci and grows exponentially: it overflows a signed 32-bit int at n = 47. LeetCode caps n at 45 precisely to hide that, which is a bad habit to pick up. In real code either return long, document the maximum supported n, or return BigInteger. Noticing the overflow boundary unprompted is usually worth more in the interview than the algorithm itself, which most candidates get.

followups.q: Can it be done faster than O(n)?
followups.a: Yes. Fibonacci can be computed by matrix exponentiation in O(log n), raising the 2x2 matrix [[1,1],[1,0]] to the nth power by repeated squaring. There is also the closed-form Binet formula, but it relies on floating point and loses accuracy above roughly n = 70, so it is unusable for exact answers. Matrix exponentiation is the real answer, and it matters when n is enormous and you are working modulo something.

followups.q: What does this problem have in common with House Robber and Coin Change?
followups.a: All three are one-dimensional DP where the state is the position and each transition looks back a fixed distance. Climbing stairs sums the ways, house robber maximises with a skip constraint, coin change minimises the count. Once you see that the recurrence shape is shared, the implementations differ only in the operator and the base case. That recognition is what interviewers are checking with this cluster of questions, which is why they often ask two of them back to back.

question: House robber: max sum with no two adjacent elements.

followups.q: Why does a greedy approach fail here?
followups.a: Because the best answer sometimes skips two houses in a row, which no local rule predicts. In [2,1,1,2] the greedy alternating pick gives 2+1 or 1+2, both 3, while the optimum takes the two ends for 4. Greedy works only when a locally optimal choice is provably part of a global optimum, and here it is not: taking a house forbids its neighbour, so the consequence of a choice extends beyond the current step. That is exactly the condition that calls for dynamic programming.

followups.q: Suppose the houses are arranged in a circle instead of a row.
followups.a: The first and last become adjacent, so they cannot both be robbed. Rather than writing a new recurrence, run the linear solution twice: once on everything except the last house, once on everything except the first, and take the larger. Each run enforces the constraint by construction. The only special case is a single house, where both slices are empty and the answer is that house's value, which is why the code checks the length first.

followups.q: Suppose the houses form a binary tree rather than a line.
followups.a: That is House Robber III, and the shape changes from a sequence to a post-order traversal. Each node returns a pair: the best total if this node is robbed, which is its value plus both children's not-robbed totals, and the best if it is not, which is the better of each child's two options summed. It is the same two-state recurrence, computed bottom-up over a tree instead of left-to-right over an array, and it is the same return-one-thing-accumulate-another shape as the tree diameter problem.

question: Coin change: fewest coins to make an amount.

followups.q: Why the Unreachable sentinel rather than filling with int.MaxValue?
followups.a: Because `best[a - coin] + 1` would overflow to int.MinValue if the entry were int.MaxValue, and Math.Min would then happily pick that negative value as the new best, silently corrupting the table. Using MaxValue - 1 and guarding with the explicit `!= Unreachable` check makes it impossible. An alternative many prefer is to fill with `amount + 1`, which is larger than any real answer yet small enough that adding one cannot overflow.

followups.q: How does coin change II, counting combinations, differ?
followups.a: It counts ways rather than minimising, and the loop order becomes load-bearing. Putting the coin loop outside and the amount loop inside counts combinations, treating 1+2 and 2+1 as the same. Swapping them counts permutations instead. The minimisation version here is indifferent to the order, which is exactly why people carry the habit over and get the counting version wrong. Being able to say which loop order gives which semantics is the whole follow-up.

followups.q: How would you return which coins were used, not just how many?
followups.a: Store the coin that produced each improvement in a parallel array, then walk backwards from the amount, subtracting each recorded coin until you reach zero. That adds O(amount) space and reconstructs in O(answer) time. It is the same parent-pointer technique used to recover a path from Dijkstra or an alignment from edit distance: the DP computes the cost, a parallel array remembers the choice, and a backward walk recovers the decisions.

question: Coin change II: number of combinations to make an amount.

followups.q: Explain why the loop order changes combinations into permutations.
followups.a: With coins outermost, the table is completed for coin 1 before coin 2 is touched, so any combination counted is built with coins in the order they appear in the list and a given multiset is reached exactly once. With the amount outermost, every coin is considered at every amount, so reaching 3 as 1-then-2 and as 2-then-1 are counted as different paths. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions, and the trap is that the code looks almost identical.

followups.q: Why does ways[0] = 1 rather than 0?
followups.a: Because there is exactly one way to make zero: choose nothing. It is the empty product, the same convention that makes 0 factorial equal 1. Setting it to 0 would make every entry zero, since every count is ultimately built from it. It is also the base case that lets a coin exactly equal to the amount be counted, which is the `Change(10, [10])` test. Getting this base case wrong produces an answer that is uniformly zero, which at least fails loudly.

followups.q: Suppose each coin were available only a limited number of times.
followups.a: That is bounded knapsack, and neither loop order handles it directly. The straightforward fix is to add an inner loop over the allowed count for each coin, making it O(coins x amount x count). The better technique is binary splitting: represent a limit of, say, 13 copies as coins of size 1, 2, 4 and 6 times the value, so any count from 0 to 13 is expressible, turning it into a 0/1 knapsack with only log(count) items. That is a genuinely useful trick and a strong answer at this level.

question: Longest increasing subsequence.

followups.q: Why is the tails array not the actual subsequence?
followups.a: Because entries are overwritten independently as better tails are found, so the array can end up holding values that never coexisted in one subsequence. For [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18] the tails end as [2,3,7,18], which happens to look plausible, but on other inputs it does not even appear in order in the original array. Only the length is guaranteed correct. To recover the actual subsequence you record, for each element, the index of its predecessor at the time it was placed, then walk those links backwards.

followups.q: What changes for a non-decreasing subsequence, where equal values are allowed?
followups.a: Switch the binary search from lower bound to upper bound: find the first tail strictly greater than the value rather than greater than or equal. With lower bound, an equal value replaces the existing tail and the length does not grow, which is what makes [7,7,7,7] answer 1. With upper bound it appends instead and the answer becomes 4. It is a one-character change in the comparison, and getting it backwards is the standard bug in this problem.

followups.q: Suppose the interviewer asks for the longest bitonic subsequence, increasing then decreasing.
followups.a: Run the O(n²) LIS forwards from every index and again backwards, then for each index i the best bitonic length through it is forward[i] + backward[i] - 1, subtracting one because i is counted twice. Take the maximum. It is a good illustration of composing a known DP rather than inventing a new recurrence, and the same forward-and-backward trick solves problems like the candy distribution and trapping rain water.

question: Longest common subsequence of two strings.

followups.q: What is the difference between a subsequence and a substring here?
followups.a: A subsequence keeps order but allows gaps, so "ace" is a subsequence of "abcde". A substring must be contiguous. The recurrences differ accordingly: for the longest common substring, a mismatch resets the cell to 0 rather than carrying the better neighbour forward, and the answer is the maximum anywhere in the table rather than the bottom-right corner. Candidates frequently solve the wrong one, so confirming which is being asked is the first move.

followups.q: How do you reduce the space to one row?
followups.a: Each cell depends only on the row above and the cell immediately to its left, so two rows suffice, and with care one row plus a saved diagonal value does. That brings it to O(min(m,n)) by iterating over the shorter string. The catch is that reconstruction becomes impossible: recovering the actual subsequence needs the full table to walk backwards. Hirschberg's algorithm solves that with divide and conquer, giving linear space and the sequence, at twice the time.

followups.q: Where is this used in real systems?
followups.a: Diff tools. `git diff` computes a longest common subsequence of the two files' lines, and everything not in it is shown as an addition or deletion. That is also why diffs on large files can be slow and why Git uses heuristics such as Myers' algorithm rather than the plain quadratic table. It also underlies DNA sequence alignment and the similarity scoring in plagiarism detection.

question: Edit distance (Levenshtein) between two strings.

followups.q: Suppose insert, delete and replace have different costs.
followups.a: Replace the three `1 +` terms with the respective costs and the recurrence still works, which is the usual weighted Levenshtein. It matters in practice: in spell checking, a replace between two adjacent keyboard keys is cheaper than between distant ones, and in DNA alignment a transition and a transversion have different penalties. One caution is that if replace costs more than an insert plus a delete, the replace branch becomes unreachable, which is a good sign the cost model needs rethinking.

followups.q: How would you add transposition, so 'ab' to 'ba' costs one rather than two?
followups.a: That is Damerau-Levenshtein, adding a fourth branch: if the current two characters are the reverse of the previous two, consider the cell two back diagonally plus one. It matters because transposition is one of the most common human typing errors, so spell checkers that ignore it rank corrections badly. The recurrence stays O(mn); only the branch count grows.

followups.q: Suppose you only need to know whether the distance is at most k, with very long strings.
followups.a: Then computing the whole table is wasteful. Because a path can only drift k cells from the diagonal without exceeding k edits, you can compute only a band of width 2k+1, giving O(k·n) rather than O(n²). That is a large saving for the typical use, since spell checkers care about distances of one or two. The short-circuit is also useful: if every value in a row exceeds k, you can stop early and report that the threshold is exceeded.

question: 0/1 knapsack: maximize value within a weight capacity.

followups.q: Explain precisely why the loop direction changes the semantics.
followups.a: When the capacity loop runs backwards, `best[c - weight]` has not yet been updated for the current item, so it still represents a solution built from earlier items only, and the item is used at most once. Running forwards, `best[c - weight]` may already include the current item, so taking it again is possible and the item becomes reusable. It is a one-character change with a completely different meaning, and being able to explain it rather than recall it is what the question is really testing.

followups.q: Is the O(items x capacity) complexity polynomial?
followups.a: Only pseudo-polynomial. The capacity appears as a magnitude, not as the size of its encoding, so a capacity of one billion makes the table enormous even though the input is short. The 0/1 knapsack is NP-hard, and this DP does not contradict that: it is efficient when the capacity is small, and useless when it is large. For large capacities you fall back on approximation schemes or branch and bound, which is worth saying because it shows you understand what the DP does and does not buy.

followups.q: Suppose you must report which items were chosen.
followups.a: The single-row version cannot tell you, because it overwrites the history. Keep the full two-dimensional table and walk backwards from the last cell: if the value differs from the cell directly above, the current item was taken, so subtract its weight and move up; otherwise just move up. That costs O(items x capacity) space instead of O(capacity). It is the same parent-tracking pattern as recovering the coin list or a Dijkstra path.

followups.q: How does partition equal subset sum relate to this?
followups.a: It is 0/1 knapsack with value equal to weight and the capacity set to half the total sum: a subset summing to half exists exactly when the knapsack can be filled precisely. An odd total is immediately impossible, which is the cheap first check. Recognising that a problem phrased about partitioning is really a knapsack in disguise is the transferable skill, and the same reframing turns target sum and last stone weight into the same algorithm.

question: Partition equal subset sum.

followups.q: Why iterate the target downwards?
followups.a: So each number is used at most once. Going downwards, `reachable[t - n]` still reflects subsets formed without the current number, because that lower index has not been updated yet in this pass. Iterating upwards would let a number contribute to `reachable[t - n]` and then immediately to `reachable[t]`, effectively using it twice, which answers a different question: whether a target is reachable with unlimited copies. It is the same loop-direction distinction as 0/1 versus unbounded knapsack.

followups.q: Suppose the array must split into three equal parts rather than two.
followups.a: It is substantially harder. The two-way version works because fixing one subset determines the other, but with three parts the subsets interact and a single boolean table no longer suffices. The usual approaches are a bitmask DP over subsets, which is exponential but feasible for small n, or backtracking with strong pruning: sort descending, place each number into the first bucket that fits, and skip buckets with identical running totals. This is the k-way partition problem and it is NP-hard in general.

followups.q: Could a bitset make this faster?
followups.a: Yes, and it is a satisfying optimisation. Represent the reachable set as a bitset and the whole inner loop becomes `bits |= bits << n`, which processes 64 targets per machine word instead of one per iteration. That gives roughly a 64-fold constant-factor speedup with no change in asymptotic complexity. C# offers this through `System.Numerics.BigInteger` shifts or a hand-rolled `ulong[]`, and it is the standard trick for subset-sum problems where the target is large.

question: Unique paths in an m×n grid (only right/down moves).

followups.q: Why interleave the multiply and divide in the closed form?
followups.a: Because computing the full factorials first overflows almost immediately: 20 factorial already exceeds a signed 64-bit integer, so a 20x20 grid would fail even though its answer fits comfortably. Multiplying by one term and dividing by the next keeps the running value close to the final answer. The division is always exact at each step, since the product of any i consecutive integers is divisible by i factorial, which is the non-obvious fact that makes the loop safe.

followups.q: Suppose some cells are blocked.
followups.a: A blocked cell contributes zero paths, so set its value to 0 and carry on; everything downstream naturally accounts for it. The one trap is the start cell being blocked, which makes the answer 0 immediately and is easy to miss when initialising. The obstacle version is the more realistic problem, and it shows why the DP is worth knowing even though the clean grid has a closed form that the DP does not generalise to.

followups.q: Suppose diagonal moves were also allowed.
followups.a: Add the diagonal predecessor to the sum, so each cell becomes above plus left plus above-left. The counts grow much faster, which is worth flagging because overflow arrives sooner. Note the closed form disappears entirely: with three move types the paths are no longer a simple choice of positions among a fixed number of moves, so the DP is the only practical route. That is a neat demonstration that a formula is a special case while the DP is the general tool.

question: Minimum path sum in a grid.

followups.q: In the rolling row, how do you know row[c] still holds the value from above?
followups.a: Because the loop moves left to right and writes each cell after reading it. When computing column c, `row[c]` has not been touched yet in this row, so it is still the previous row's value, which is the cell above; `row[c-1]` was written a moment ago, so it is the current row's cell to the left. That read-before-write ordering is the whole trick, and reversing the loop direction would silently break it, which is a good thing to state rather than leave implicit.

followups.q: Suppose movement in all four directions were allowed, not just right and down.
followups.a: The DP collapses, because a cell could be reached from a cell you have not computed yet, so there is no valid evaluation order. It becomes a shortest-path problem on a graph with non-negative weights, which is Dijkstra with a priority queue, at O(rc log(rc)). This is the cleanest illustration of when a grid DP stops applying: DP needs a partial order on the subproblems, and free movement destroys it.

followups.q: Suppose some cells had negative values.
followups.a: With only right and down moves the DP still works, because the move set forbids revisiting a cell and so no negative cycle can form. If free movement were also allowed, negative values would break Dijkstra and you would need Bellman-Ford, and a negative cycle would mean no minimum exists at all. Pointing out that the answer depends on both the sign of the weights and the freedom of movement, rather than just one of them, is the strong version of this answer.

question: Best time to buy/sell stock with cooldown (or with transaction fee).
answer: State machine DP with states: hold, sold (cooldown), rest. Transitions: hold = max(hold, rest - price); sold = hold + price; rest = max(rest, sold). Iterate over prices tracking these. O(n) time, O(1) space. With a fee, subtract it on sell.

question: Word break II: return all sentences from segmenting a string.
answer: DFS with memoization: for each start index, try each dictionary word prefix, recurse on the remainder, and prepend the word to each returned sentence. Cache results per start index. Exponential outputs but memoization avoids recomputation. Combine with a word-break feasibility check to prune.

question: Longest palindromic subsequence.
answer: dp[i][j] = LPS in s[i..j]. If s[i]==s[j], dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j-1] + 2, else max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Fill by increasing substring length. O(n^2) time and space. Equivalent to LCS of s and its reverse.

question: Decode ways (number of ways to decode a digit string).
answer: dp[i] = ways to decode the first i digits. Add dp[i-1] if the current digit is 1-9, and dp[i-2] if the last two digits form 10-26. Handle leading zeros (invalid). O(n) time, O(1) space with two variables.

question: Maximal square: largest square of 1s in a binary matrix.

followups.q: Why the minimum of three neighbours rather than, say, the smaller of two?
followups.a: Because a square of side k at a corner requires a square of side k-1 to exist in all three directions simultaneously. Using only the cell above and to the left would allow an L-shaped region to be counted as a square: imagine a full row and a full column meeting at a corner with a hole in between. The diagonal neighbour is what certifies the interior is filled. Dropping it is the classic wrong answer and it passes every test case with no holes.

followups.q: Suppose it asked for the largest rectangle rather than the largest square.
followups.a: The DP does not generalise, because a rectangle has two independent dimensions and the min-of-three trick relies on a single one. The standard solution treats each row as the base of a histogram of consecutive 1s above it, then runs the largest-rectangle-in-a-histogram algorithm per row using a monotonic stack, giving O(rows x cols). It is a genuinely different technique, which is why interviewers sometimes ask the square first and the rectangle as the escalation.

followups.q: Why pad the table with an extra row and column?
followups.a: So that cells on the first row or column can read their neighbours without a boundary check. The padded zeros correctly represent 'no square beyond the edge', which is exactly the right value, so correctness and convenience agree. It costs one extra row and column of memory and removes four conditionals from the hot loop. The offset by one between matrix and table indices is the price, and it is the usual source of confusion when reading this kind of code.

question: Target sum: count ways to assign +/- to reach a target.
answer: Transform to subset-sum: find a subset with sum (total + target)/2 (must be a non-negative integer). Count subsets reaching that sum with a 1D DP (dp[s] += dp[s-num]). O(n * sum) time. Handle impossible parity/overflow cases.

question: Regular expression / wildcard matching with DP.
answer: dp[i][j] = does s[0..i) match p[0..j). For '?' or a matching char, dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]; for '*', dp[i][j] = dp[i][j-1] (empty) or dp[i-1][j] (consume one char). Initialize dp[0][j] for leading stars. O(m*n) time and space.

question: Number of longest increasing subsequences (count of LIS).
answer: Two DP arrays: length[i] = LIS ending at i, count[i] = number of such LIS. When extending from j to i, if it forms a longer LIS update length and copy count; if equal length, add counts. Sum counts of the max length. O(n^2) time.

question: Generate all subsets (the power set).

followups.q: Why copy current into a new list rather than adding it directly?
followups.a: Because `current` is a single mutable list that the recursion keeps changing. Adding it by reference would put the same object into the result eight times, and every entry would end up showing whatever state it held at the end, typically empty. It is the classic aliasing bug in backtracking, and it produces output that is uniformly wrong rather than subtly wrong, which at least makes it easy to spot. The copy is what makes each recorded subset a snapshot.

followups.q: Suppose the input contains duplicates and subsets must be unique.
followups.a: Sort first, then in the loop skip any element equal to the previous one at the same recursion depth, using `if (i > index && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue;`. Sorting puts equal values adjacent so the check is local, and the `i > index` part is essential: it allows a duplicate to be used at a deeper level, where it legitimately extends a subset, while preventing it from starting a second identical branch at the same level. Getting that condition wrong either produces duplicates or drops valid subsets.

followups.q: When would you choose the bitmask version?
followups.a: When n is at most about 20 to 30 and you want iteration without recursion, which avoids stack depth and is easier to parallelise since each mask is independent. It is also the natural representation for bitmask DP, where a subset is a state, as in the travelling salesman DP. The limit is real though: at n = 31 the shift overflows a signed int, and the enumeration itself is already astronomically large well before that, so in practice n is small whenever this approach applies at all.

question: Generate all permutations of a list.

followups.q: Explain the duplicate-skipping condition, especially the !used[i-1] part.
followups.a: After sorting, equal values are adjacent. The rule is that among a run of identical values, they must be used left to right; picking a later duplicate while its identical predecessor is still unused would generate a permutation already produced by the mirror choice. So `!used[i-1]` detects exactly that situation and prunes it. Writing `used[i-1]` instead inverts the logic and drops valid permutations, which is the standard mistake. The condition is small and the reasoning is not, so it is worth deriving on a [1,1,2] example rather than reciting.

followups.q: Suppose you need the next permutation in lexicographic order rather than all of them.
followups.a: That is a different, much cheaper algorithm: scan from the right for the first element smaller than its successor, find the rightmost element greater than it, swap them, then reverse the suffix. It is O(n) time and O(1) space, and it is what `std::next_permutation` does. When you only need to iterate permutations one at a time, or when n is large enough that n! is out of the question, generating the next one on demand is the right tool.

followups.q: How does the swap-based version differ, and why might you avoid it?
followups.a: It permutes the array in place by swapping the current index with each later index, which avoids the `used` array and the per-level allocation. It is slightly faster, but it destroys the relative order of the remaining elements, so the output is not lexicographic even for sorted input, and the duplicate-skipping trick no longer works because equal values are no longer reliably adjacent. For the unique-permutations variant the `used` array version is the one to reach for.

question: Combination sum: find combinations that sum to a target (reuse allowed).

followups.q: Why does passing i rather than i + 1 give reuse, and why not pass 0?
followups.a: Passing `i` lets the current candidate be chosen again at the next level, which is the reuse the problem wants. Passing `0` would also allow reuse but would additionally revisit earlier candidates, generating [2,3] and [3,2] as separate results. Starting at `i` forces every combination to be built in non-decreasing order, so each multiset is produced exactly once. That is the same ordering trick that makes the coin-change combination count work, seen from the enumeration side.

followups.q: Why break rather than continue when the candidate overshoots?
followups.a: Because the array is sorted, so if candidates[i] already exceeds the remaining target, every candidate after it exceeds it too and the rest of the loop is guaranteed to be fruitless. `continue` would test each of them individually, which is correct but wasteful. On inputs with many large candidates the difference is substantial, and it is the main reason to sort at all here, since sorting is not needed for correctness.

followups.q: Suppose each candidate may be used at most once, and the input contains duplicates.
followups.a: That is Combination Sum II, and it needs two changes: recurse with `i + 1` so each element is consumed, and skip duplicates at the same level with `if (i > start && candidates[i] == candidates[i-1]) continue;`. The `i > start` guard is what distinguishes 'this is a repeat of a sibling choice' from 'this is a legitimate second copy deeper in the tree'. It is the same pruning condition as in subsets-with-duplicates, which is worth pointing out as the shared pattern.

question: Combinations: choose k numbers from 1..n.
answer: Backtracking from a start value: pick a number, recurse increasing the start, and stop when k are chosen. Prune when not enough numbers remain to complete a combination. C(n,k) results. Depth k, branching bounded by remaining numbers.

question: N-Queens: place N queens so none attack each other.

followups.q: Why do row - col and row + col identify the diagonals?
followups.a: Moving one step down-right increases both row and column by one, so their difference is unchanged along that diagonal. Moving down-left increases the row and decreases the column, so their sum is unchanged. That gives each diagonal a constant identifier, turning an O(n) scan along the diagonal into an O(1) array lookup. Adding n to the difference shifts the range from -(n-1)..(n-1) into 0..2n-2 so it can index an array, which is the only reason the offset is there.

followups.q: Suppose you only need the count, not the boards.
followups.a: Drop the rendering and the placement array, and the natural optimisation is a bitmask version: hold the three conflict sets as integers and use bit operations to compute all available columns at once, picking the lowest set bit each time. That removes the loop's repeated checks and is dramatically faster, comfortably handling n = 15 or so. Beyond that the count grows too fast for exhaustive search regardless of constant factors, and the known values come from specialised methods.

followups.q: Why are n = 2 and n = 3 impossible?
followups.a: For n = 2, one queen on a 2x2 board attacks every remaining square. For n = 3, wherever the first queen goes, the remaining rows cannot both be filled without a diagonal or column conflict; exhausting the nine placements shows it. Solutions exist for n = 1 and for every n of 4 or more. It is worth stating because a candidate who only tests n = 8 may write code that silently mishandles the no-solution case, and returning an empty list rather than throwing is the right behaviour.

followups.q: How would you exploit the board's symmetry?
followups.a: Solutions come in symmetry classes under the eight rotations and reflections of the square, so you can restrict the first queen to the left half of the first row and mirror the results, roughly halving the search. Full exploitation means canonicalising each solution under the symmetry group and expanding at the end, which is how published counts are computed efficiently. It is a good example of cutting a search by exploiting problem structure rather than by micro-optimising the inner loop.

question: Sudoku solver.
answer: Backtracking: find an empty cell, try digits 1-9 that don't violate row/column/box constraints (track with sets or boolean arrays), place and recurse; undo on failure. Return true when the board is filled. Constraint propagation / choosing the most-constrained cell speeds it up.

question: Letter combinations of a phone number.

followups.q: Why must the empty input return an empty list rather than a list with one empty string?
followups.a: Because mathematically there is exactly one function from an empty set, so the product is arguably a single empty combination, but the problem statement specifies an empty result and callers expect that. It matters more than it sounds: the recursion naturally produces the single empty string, so you have to guard against it explicitly. That mismatch between the mathematically natural answer and the specified one is worth confirming rather than assuming, and it is the single most common way this easy problem is failed.

followups.q: Would you write this iteratively instead?
followups.a: You can, and it is clean: start with a list containing one empty string, then for each digit replace the list with every existing prefix extended by every letter for that digit. It is a breadth-first construction rather than depth-first, needs no recursion, and is easy to read. The trade-off is memory: it materialises every intermediate level, so at the last digit it holds the full result plus the previous level, whereas backtracking holds only one path at a time.

followups.q: Suppose this fed a real autocomplete over a dictionary, not just raw combinations.
followups.a: Then generating all combinations first is wasteful, since almost all of them are not words. Instead walk a trie of the dictionary in lockstep with the digits: at each digit, extend only those trie nodes that have a child for one of that digit's letters, pruning dead branches immediately. That is how T9 predictive text worked, and it turns an exponential enumeration into a search bounded by the number of real words sharing that prefix.

question: Generate valid parentheses combinations of n pairs.

followups.q: How many results are there, and why does that number appear so often?
followups.a: The nth Catalan number: 1, 2, 5, 14, 42 for n = 1 to 5. It counts balanced bracket sequences, and also the number of distinct binary search trees on n nodes, the triangulations of a polygon, and the ways to parenthesise a product. They are all the same counting problem in disguise, which is why 'count unique BSTs' and this question have identical answers. Recognising the sequence is a good signal that you have seen the structure before.

followups.q: Why is this considered better than generate-and-filter?
followups.a: Because the constraints are applied during construction rather than afterwards, so invalid branches are never explored. For n = 3, filtering would examine 64 strings to keep 5; the constrained search touches only the nodes leading to valid results. The saving grows exponentially with n. It is the defining characteristic of backtracking as opposed to brute-force enumeration: prune as early as the constraint can be evaluated, not at the leaves.

followups.q: Suppose there were multiple bracket types, as in a real expression.
followups.a: The single open-count no longer suffices, because closing must match the most recent unclosed opener, so you carry a stack of open types instead. You may open any type at any time while budget remains, and may close only the type on top of the stack. The count grows much faster since each opening choice multiplies the branching. That variant is closer to generating syntactically valid expressions, and it is a natural escalation for a candidate who solves the single-type version quickly.

question: Word search in a grid (single word).

followups.q: Why restore the cell rather than keep a visited set for the whole search?
followups.a: Because the exclusion is per path, not global. A cell used by one candidate path must remain available to a different path starting elsewhere, so a permanent visited marker would wrongly reject valid words. This is the defining difference between backtracking and flood fill: flood fill marks permanently because it is partitioning the grid, whereas here the grid is a search space each path traverses independently.

followups.q: Suppose you must find many words in the same grid, not one.
followups.a: Running this per word is O(words x rc x 4^L), which is far too slow. The right answer is Word Search II: build a trie of all the words, then do a single DFS from each cell walking the trie in lockstep with the grid, so a path is abandoned the moment no word continues with that prefix. One traversal finds every word, and pruning completed words from the trie keeps it shrinking. That is a standard escalation once a candidate solves the single-word version.

followups.q: Using '\0' as the marker mutates the caller's board. Is that acceptable?
followups.a: It is restored before returning, so the board is unchanged on exit, and it avoids allocating a visited grid. But it is not exception-safe: if anything threw mid-search the board would be left corrupted, and it is not thread-safe, since two concurrent searches would see each other's markers. For an interview it is the expected answer; for shared or concurrent code I would use a separate visited array and say so. The marker also assumes '\0' never appears as real data, which is the usual in-band sentinel caveat.

question: Palindrome partitioning: all ways to split into palindromes.
